FERPO: Forward Entropy-Regularized
Policy Optimization

Sebastian Sanokowski Affiliation: Applied and Theoretical Aspects of Robot Intelligence (ATARI) Lab    Alireza Sarmadi Affiliation: Munich Institute of Robotics and Machine Intelligence (MIRMI)    Majid Khadiv Affiliation: Technical University of Munich
Abstract

Several state-of-the-art methods for online reinforcement learning in continuous control improve policies using action gradients of a learned critic. However, critics are typically trained to predict returns, and accurate value predictions do not necessarily yield accurate action derivatives, potentially leading to unreliable policy updates. We propose Forward Entropy-Regularized Policy Optimization (FERPO), an on-policy maximum entropy reinforcement learning algorithm that performs policy improvement using critic values without differentiating the critic with respect to actions. FERPO derives an optimal target action distribution from a policy-improvement objective regularized by entropy and Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence. We then fit the actor to this target by minimizing a forward-KL objective, estimated using self-normalized importance sampling (SNIS) with actions drawn from the rollout policy. By limiting the target distribution’s deviation from the rollout policy, the KL regularization helps keep these importance weights well behaved. In contrast to reverse-KL objectives, which can favor a subset of the target distribution’s modes, the forward-KL objective encourages coverage of multiple high-value modes and thereby promotes exploration. Experiments and ablations on MuJoCo Playground and ManiSkill show competitive performance and sample-efficiency gains. Computational benchmarks also demonstrate faster actor updates than Relative Entropy Pathwise Policy Optimization (REPPO). Our implementation is publicly available.11 1 Code: https://github.com/Atarilab/FERPO.

1 Introduction

Reinforcement learning (RL) learns policies through interaction to maximize cumulative reward. Its successes range from game playing (?) to autonomous drone racing (?) and robot locomotion (?). In robotics, massively parallel simulation has accelerated on-policy learning by collecting trajectories from thousands of environments simultaneously. This has enabled rapid policy training and successful transfer from simulation to physical robots (??). These advances make efficient and reliable policy improvement central to scaling online robot learning.

Relative Entropy Pathwise Policy Optimization (REPPO; ?) is a recent state-of-the-art on-policy method for this setting. It learns a soft action-value critic from on-policy trajectories and improves the actor by differentiating the critic with respect to actions, while limiting policy changes relative to the rollout policy. This makes pathwise actor updates compatible with massively parallel on-policy learning. However, standard critic training supervises values, whereas these actor updates require accurate action derivatives. Accurate value predictions do not necessarily imply accurate derivatives: critic-gradient error can bias policy improvement (?), and learned action gradients can show poor directional agreement with rollout-based estimates (?). In on-policy learning, biased gradients can also interact with changing data distributions and destabilize training (?). These limitations motivate policy improvement that uses critic values without requiring their action derivatives.

We derive the optimal target distribution for a standard RL policy-improvement objective with entropy and Kullback–Leibler (KL) regularization. Making this target explicit lets us replace reverse-KL projection by forward-KL fitting, which encourages coverage of target modes (?). The KL trust region keeps the target close to the rollout policy, helping control importance-weight concentration, as in recent diffusion and normalizing flow based sampling methods (??). We introduce Forward Entropy-Regularized Policy Optimization (FERPO), which applies this construction to on-policy learning. Its actor update uses critic values without differentiating the critic with respect to actions. Our contributions are:

  • •

    An on-policy actor update that uses critic values to construct a regularized target action distribution and fits the actor to this target using forward KL, without differentiating the critic with respect to actions (Section 3.1).

  • •

    A practical estimator using self-normalized importance sampling (SNIS), with Lagrange multipliers that regulate policy entropy and importance-weight concentration through normalized effective sample size (ESS) (Sections 3.1 and 3.2).

  • •

    An evaluation on ManiSkill and MuJoCo Playground demonstrating competitive performance and sample-efficiency gains (Section 5.4), supported by ablations (Section 5.3) and computational benchmarks showing faster actor updates than REPPO (Section 5.2).

  • •

    Cached actor updates that reduce computation, and a state-value extension based on one-step simulation, with promising results on AcrobotSwingupSparse (Section 5.3).

Let πroll:=πθroll\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}:=\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{roll}}} be the frozen policy that generated the current rollout, with soft critic Qroll:=QτπrollQ_{\mathrm{roll}}:=Q_{\tau}^{\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}}. Applying the policy-gradient theorem (?) to Eq. 1 yields the local reverse-KL surrogate

ℒME(θ;θroll):=τ1−γ𝔼s∼droll[DKL(πθ(⋅∣s)∥pQ,τ(⋅∣s))],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ME}}(\theta;\theta_{\mathrm{roll}}):=\frac{\tau}{1-\gamma}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\mathrm{roll}}}\!\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s)\middle\|p_{Q,\tau}(\cdot\mid s)\right)\right], (2)

Δ​Jτ≥Δ​Jsurrogate−4​γ​ϵA(1−γ)2​(DTVmax)2−τ1−γ​DKLmax,\Delta J_{\tau}\geq\Delta J_{\mathrm{surrogate}}-\frac{4\gamma\epsilon_{A}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}(D_{\mathrm{TV}}^{\max})^{2}-\frac{\tau}{1-\gamma}D_{\mathrm{KL}}^{\max}, (3)

where DKLmax:=supsDKL(πcurr(⋅∣s)∥πroll(⋅∣s))D_{\mathrm{KL}}^{\max}:=\sup_{s}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\mathrm{curr}}(\cdot\mid s)\|\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(\cdot\mid s)). The TV term bounds the advantage error; the KL term is the entropy correction (Appendix B.6). This motivates minimizing ℒME\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ME}} subject to DKLmax≤δKLD_{\mathrm{KL}}^{\max}\leq\delta_{\mathrm{KL}}. For tanh-squashed Gaussians, as frequently used in MaxEnt-RL, uniform forward-KL constraints or TV bounds strictly below one also control the reverse-KL entropy correction (Appendix B.7).

Practical objective. Replacing the supremum by an expectation over rollout states gives the average-KL constraint D¯θ:=𝔼s∼droll[DKL(πθ(⋅∣s)∥πroll(⋅∣s))]≤δKL\bar{D}_{\theta}:=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\mathrm{roll}}}[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s)\|\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(\cdot\mid s))]\leq\delta_{\mathrm{KL}}. We also require a minimum average entropy ℋ¯θ:=𝔼s∼droll[ℋ(πθ(⋅∣s))]≥ℋtarget\bar{\mathcal{H}}_{\theta}:=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\mathrm{roll}}}[\mathcal{H}(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s))]\geq\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{target}}, interpreting τ\tau as its Lagrange multiplier, as in automatic entropy tuning (?). With QrollQ_{\mathrm{roll}} and drolld_{\mathrm{roll}} held fixed, maximizing expected critic value under these constraints gives the Lagrangian

ℒ⁡(πθ,τ,λ):=−𝔼s∼drolla∼πθ(⋅∣s)​[Qroll​(s,a)]+τ⁡(ℋtarget−ℋ¯θ)+λ⁡(D¯θ−δKL),\mathcal{L}(\pi_{\theta},\tau,\lambda):=-\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}s\sim d_{\mathrm{roll}}\\ a\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s)\end{subarray}}[Q_{\mathrm{roll}}(s,a)]+\tau(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{target}}-\bar{\mathcal{H}}_{\theta})+\lambda(\bar{D}_{\theta}-\delta_{\mathrm{KL}}), (4)

where τ,λ≥0\tau,\lambda\geq 0. The policy minimizes ℒ\mathcal{L}, while the multipliers maximize it: τ\tau increases when entropy is below target, and λ\lambda increases when the KL bound is exceeded. The rollout-average constraint and estimated critic approximate the trust-region problem but do not guarantee its worst-state bound. This motivates a shared design principle for practical on-policy algorithms: control deviation from the rollout policy when making multiple updates on the same data, so that the local surrogate remains informative.

Connection to existing methods. TRPO controls policy changes through an explicit KL constraint (?), while Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) clips policy likelihood ratios in the actor surrogate to discourage large changes (?). Relative entropy pathwise policy optimization (REPPO) learns a soft critic QϕQ_{\phi} from on-policy rollouts. At each state, let k^θ​(s)\widehat{k}_{\theta}(s) estimate the forward KL DKL(πroll(⋅∣s)∥πθ(⋅∣s))D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(\cdot\mid s)\|\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s)), using actions drawn from πroll\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}. For k^θ​(s)<δKL\widehat{k}_{\theta}(s)<\delta_{\mathrm{KL}}, REPPO minimizes the unconstrained loss ℓME(θ;s)=𝔼a∼πθ(⋅∣s)[τlogπθ(a∣s)−Qϕ(s,a)]\ell_{\mathrm{ME}}(\theta;s)=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s)}[\tau\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)-Q_{\phi}(s,a)] using pathwise gradients. Otherwise, it replaces this loss by λ​k^θ​(s)\lambda\widehat{k}_{\theta}(s), with adaptive λ>0\lambda>0, pulling the policy back toward πroll\pi_{\mathrm{roll}} (?).

3 Method: FERPO

Pathwise actor updates require accurate critic action derivatives, although standard critic learning supervises values. Value accuracy alone does not ensure derivative accuracy (??). This motivates an actor update that uses critic values without requiring ∇aQϕ​(s,a)\nabla_{a}Q_{\phi}(s,a). We introduce Forward Entropy-Regularized Policy Optimization (FERPO). FERPO first minimizes the Lagrangian in Eq. 4 over unrestricted action distributions q(⋅∣s)q(\cdot\mid s) with fixed multipliers, then fits the parametric policy to the resulting target using the forward KL divergence combined with self-normalized importance sampling (SNIS). The temperature and trust-region multiplier are adapted alongside the actor. The actor differentiates the policy log density with the target weights held fixed; it still depends on critic-value accuracy and adequate sampling of the target.

3.1 Target construction and actor updates

We define the target as q∗=arg⁡minq⁡ℒ⁡(q,τ,λ)q^{*}=\arg\min_{q}\mathcal{L}(q,\tau,\lambda), with ℒ\mathcal{L} from Eq. 4 and the minimization over all conditional action densities q(⋅∣s)q(\cdot\mid s), unrestricted by the parametric policy family. With the critic, rollout policy, τ\tau, and λ\lambda fixed, this minimization separates across states. Introducing a Lagrange multiplier for the normalization constraint ∫𝒜q⁡(a∣s)​𝑑a=1\int_{\mathcal{A}}q(a\mid s)\,\mathrm{d}a=1 and setting the functional derivative with respect to qq to zero yields the unique optimal density

q∗​(a∣s)=1Z∗​(s)​exp⁡(Qroll​(s,a)τ+λ)​πroll​(a∣s)λ/(τ+λ).q^{*}(a\mid s)=\frac{1}{Z_{*}(s)}\exp\!\left(\frac{Q_{\mathrm{roll}}(s,a)}{\tau+\lambda}\right)\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(a\mid s)^{\lambda/(\tau+\lambda)}. (5)

Here Z∗​(s)Z_{*}(s) normalizes the density. Thus, q∗q^{*} is the unrestricted minimizer of ℒ⁡(⋅,τ,λ)\mathcal{L}(\cdot,\tau,\lambda), which we subsequently approximate within the policy family. See Appendix B.2 for a derivation. The target combines high-value actions with proximity to the rollout policy: λ=0\lambda=0 recovers pQ,τp_{Q,\tau}, while increasing λ\lambda makes the update more conservative. Under the assumptions of Appendix B.4, repeated exact unrestricted updates with a fixed critic and temperature and a refreshed reference converge to pQ,τp_{Q,\tau}. The fixed KL multiplier λ\lambda controls the convergence rate without changing the limit.

For fixed multipliers, Eq. 4 equals (τ+λ)𝔼s∼droll[DKL(πθ∥q∗)](\tau+\lambda)\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\mathrm{roll}}}[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}\|q^{*})] plus a constant independent of the policy. FERPO replaces this reverse-KL projection by a forward-KL fit, keeping the critic and rollout parameters fixed during each actor update:

ℒF(θ):=𝔼s∼droll[DKL(q∗(⋅∣s)∥πθ(⋅∣s))]=−𝔼s∼drolla∼q∗(⋅∣s)[logπθ(a∣s)]+const.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{F}}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\mathrm{roll}}}\!\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(q^{*}(\cdot\mid s)\middle\|\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s)\right)\right]=-\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}s\sim d_{\mathrm{roll}}\\ a\sim q^{*}(\cdot\mid s)\end{subarray}}[\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)]+\mathrm{const}.

This is a weighted maximum-likelihood fit to the optimal regularized target. All state expectations below use the frozen distribution drolld_{\mathrm{roll}} and are estimated using rollout batches. To estimate the action expectation, draw KK candidate actions ai∼πroll(⋅∣s)a_{i}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(\cdot\mid s) and minimize the SNIS loss

ℒ^F​(θ):=−𝔼s∼droll​[∑i=1Kwi​(s)​log⁡πθ​(ai∣s)],wherewi​(s):=exp⁡(ℓi​(s))∑j=1Kexp⁡(ℓj​(s)),\boxed{\widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{F}}(\theta):=-\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\mathrm{roll}}}\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{K}w_{i}(s)\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{i}\mid s)\right],\quad\text{where}\quad w_{i}(s):=\frac{\exp(\ell_{i}(s))}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(\ell_{j}(s))}}, (6)

with ℓi​(s):=[Qϕ​(s,ai)−τ​log⁡πroll​(ai∣s)]/(τ+λ)\ell_{i}(s):=[Q_{\phi}(s,a_{i})-\tau\log\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(a_{i}\mid s)]/(\tau+\lambda). The weights are held fixed during the actor update.

Multiplier losses and complete actor update. As suggested by Eq. 4, we adapt the temperature τ\tau and trust-region coefficient λ\lambda as Lagrange multipliers alongside the policy. We parameterize τ=exp⁡(η)\tau=\exp(\eta) and λ=exp⁡(ξ)\lambda=\exp(\xi) to keep both multipliers positive. The temperature update follows automatic entropy tuning in SAC (?). Using fresh actions a~s∼πθ(⋅∣s)\widetilde{a}_{s}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s), we estimate the policy entropy as ℋ^θ:=−𝔼s∼droll​[log⁡πθ​(a~s∣s)]\widehat{\mathcal{H}}_{\theta}:=-\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\mathrm{roll}}}[\log\pi_{\theta}(\widetilde{a}_{s}\mid s)] and minimize

ℒτ​(η):=τ​stopgrad⁡[ℋ^θ−ℋtarget],\mathcal{L}_{\tau}(\eta):=\tau\,\operatorname{stopgrad}[\widehat{\mathcal{H}}_{\theta}-\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{target}}], (7)

where stopgrad\operatorname{stopgrad} holds its argument fixed during differentiation. Gradient descent increases τ\tau when entropy is below ℋtarget\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{target}} and decreases it when entropy exceeds the target.

For λ\lambda, however, we replace direct KL control with an update based on the log normalized effective sample size (ESS) of the importance weights. This regulates weight concentration; Section 3.2 gives the detailed motivation and its connection to trust-region control. Using the weights from Eq. 6, define e^​(s):=(K​∑i=1Kwi​(s)2)−1\widehat{e}(s):=(K\sum_{i=1}^{K}w_{i}(s)^{2})^{-1}, which ranges from 1/K1/K when one action carries all weight to 11 for uniform weights. For K≥2K\geq 2 and a target etarget∈(1/K,1)e_{\mathrm{target}}\in(1/K,1), we minimize

ℒλ​(ξ):=λ​stopgrad⁡[𝔼s∼droll​[log⁡e^​(s)]−log⁡etarget].\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}(\xi):=\lambda\,\operatorname{stopgrad}\!\left[\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\mathrm{roll}}}[\log\widehat{e}(s)]-\log e_{\mathrm{target}}\right]. (8)

This increases λ\lambda when average log ESS falls below log⁡etarget\log e_{\mathrm{target}}, flattening the weights, and decreases it when average log ESS exceeds the target. Together with the forward fit, these multiplier losses give the complete actor objective

ℒpolicy​(θ,η,ξ):=ℒ^F​(θ)+ℒτ​(η)+ℒλ​(ξ).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{policy}}(\theta,\eta,\xi):=\widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{F}}(\theta)+\mathcal{L}_{\tau}(\eta)+\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}(\xi).

The weights are detached from both the policy and multipliers, and the entropy and log-ESS gaps are detached in their respective losses. The critic and rollout policy stay fixed within each actor update; updated τ\tau and λ\lambda are used to construct the next target weights. Algorithm 1 in Appendix A.4 summarizes the full training loop.

3.2 Log ESS and trust-region control

Controlling importance-weight concentration. Using the optimal regularized distribution q∗q^{*} as the forward-KL target tempers the importance weights needed to fit the Boltzmann target pQ,τp_{Q,\tau} directly. For τ>0\tau>0, q∗​(a∣s)/πroll​(a∣s)∝[pQ,τ​(a∣s)/πroll​(a∣s)]τ/(τ+λ)q^{*}(a\mid s)/\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(a\mid s)\propto[p_{Q,\tau}(a\mid s)/\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(a\mid s)]^{\tau/(\tau+\lambda)}. For λ>0\lambda>0, the exponent lies below one, reducing log-weight differences and flattening the normalized weights on the same candidate actions. With zero entropy regularization (τ=0\tau=0, λ>0\lambda>0), the explicit rollout-density factor cancels entirely, leaving wi​(s)∝exp⁡(Qϕ​(s,ai)/λ)w_{i}(s)\propto\exp(Q_{\phi}(s,a_{i})/\lambda). For positive τ\tau, the residual factor is πroll(ai∣s)−τ/(τ+λ)\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(a_{i}\mid s)^{-\tau/(\tau+\lambda)}. For a fixed critic and rollout policy, increasing τ\tau at fixed λ\lambda strengthens this inverse-density dependence and can increase weight concentration, although it also softens the value weighting, so the overall effect need not be monotone. The update of the Lagrange multiplier λ\lambda in Eq. 8 uses this flattening effect to limit weight concentration.

At the population level, a lower bound on normalized ESS also gives an upper bound on the target’s KL divergence from the rollout policy. The following proposition also transfers this control to the fitted actor in TV when its population fitting loss does not increase. This motivates using ESS to adapt λ\lambda and connects it to the policy-proximity motivation in Section 2.

Proposition 1 (ESS control of target and actor).

Fix a state and a target q∗≪πrollq^{*}\ll\pi_{\mathrm{roll}} with population normalized ESS e∞:=1/𝔼πroll​[(q∗/πroll)2]>0e_{\infty}:=1/\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}}[(q^{*}/\pi_{\mathrm{roll}})^{2}]>0. If fitting to this fixed target satisfies DKL(q∗∥πcurr)≤DKL(q∗∥πroll)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q^{*}\|\pi_{\mathrm{curr}})\leq D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q^{*}\|\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}), the triangle inequality and Pinsker’s inequality give

12DTV(πcurr,πroll)2≤DKL(q∗∥πroll)≤D2(q∗∥πroll)=−loge∞,\frac{1}{2}D_{\mathrm{TV}}(\pi_{\mathrm{curr}},\pi_{\mathrm{roll}})^{2}\leq D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q^{*}\|\pi_{\mathrm{roll}})\leq D_{2}(q^{*}\|\pi_{\mathrm{roll}})=-\log e_{\infty}, (9)

where D2D_{2} is the order-two Rényi divergence (?).

The proof is given in Appendix B.3. What the ESS target controls. FERPO uses a shared λ\lambda to regulate log ESS averaged over rollout states. Under the population fitting condition, higher population ESS tightens the bound on the total variation between πcurr\pi_{\mathrm{curr}} and πroll\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}. For Gaussian policies, a uniform TV bound below one also bounds DKL(πcurr∥πroll)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\mathrm{curr}}\|\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}). In practice, ESS is estimated from sampled actions and averaged across states, so the controller does not guarantee this KL bound at every state.

3.3 Critic learning

To improve learning of the soft action-value function QϕQ_{\phi}, we follow the critic-training approach of REPPO (?), combining multi-step temporal-difference (TD) targets with trace parameter λTD\lambda_{\mathrm{TD}}, the histogram loss with Gaussian targets (HL-Gauss) (?), and auxiliary prediction losses. The targets are computed from on-policy rollouts and include the entropy contributions to the soft return. Here λTD\lambda_{\mathrm{TD}} is the trace-decay parameter, separate from the actor’s KL coefficient λ\lambda. HL-Gauss encodes each scalar soft-return target as a Gaussian-smoothed histogram over value bins and trains the critic’s categorical output using cross-entropy. The scalar Qϕ​(s,a)Q_{\phi}(s,a) is recovered as the mean of the predicted histogram. Following REPPO, auxiliary self-prediction trains the critic representation to predict the next transition’s latent representation, providing an additional learning signal alongside the value targets (???).

4 Related Work

Constrained measure transport (CMT). Related methods use similar constrained target construction and distribution fitting for sampling with normalizing flows (?) and diffusion models (?). Both adapt the trust-region multiplier λ\lambda using KL constraints. The normalizing-flow method additionally regulates temperature through a bound on entropy decrease.

Maximum a posteriori policy optimization. MPO is an off-policy method that alternates KL-constrained target construction with forward-KL policy fitting, using replay data and Retrace for critic learning (?). Using our notation, its variational objective uses the augmented reward r⁡(s,a)−λ​log⁡(q⁡(a∣s)/πroll​(a∣s))r(s,a)-\lambda\log(q(a\mid s)/\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(a\mid s)), with unrestricted improvement distribution qq and frozen reference policy πroll\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}. In MPO, this reference can differ from the behavior policies represented in replay. On-policy MPO would set q=πrollq=\pi_{\mathrm{roll}} where the log ratio vanishes, so its critic estimates unregularized environment returns. MPO uses a KL constraint to limit the improvement of qq away from πroll\pi_{\mathrm{roll}} while this critic is held fixed (?). FERPO also uses forward-KL fitting, but learns from on-policy rollouts with the entropy-augmented return r⁡(s,a)−τ​log⁡πθ​(a∣s)r(s,a)-\tau\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s). Its critic therefore retains future entropy contributions even when evaluating the rollout policy, while a separate λ\lambda controls policy deviation during improvement.

Advantage-weighted policy fitting. Advantage-weighted regression (AWR; ?) and advantage-weighted actor–critic (AWAC; ?) are off-policy methods that fit policies to actions stored in replay using exponential advantage weights. AWR can learn online from scratch, while AWAC targets offline pretraining followed by online fine-tuning. Their underlying target is q∗​(a∣s)∝πbeh​(a∣s)​exp⁡(Aenv​(s,a)/λ)q^{*}(a\mid s)\propto\pi_{\mathrm{beh}}(a\mid s)\exp(A_{\mathrm{env}}(s,a)/\lambda), where πbeh\pi_{\mathrm{beh}} is the conditional action distribution represented in replay, potentially combining multiple behavior policies, and AenvA_{\mathrm{env}} estimates unregularized advantage. The state-dependent advantage baseline cancels on normalization, so FERPO at τ=0\tau=0 has the same target for a common reference and critic. AWR and AWAC omit the state-dependent normalizer, thereby reweighting states in the policy-fitting objective (see Appendix A.5 for details). FERPO instead learns from fresh on-policy rollouts, samples candidate actions from the frozen rollout policy, and uses SNIS to normalize their weights separately within each state. For τ>0\tau>0, FERPO also favors less likely actions at equal critic value, providing an explicit exploration incentive.

5 Experiments

5.1 Update directions and sampling

We compare actor updates on the bimodal cost c⁡(a)=(a2−1)2−0.1​ac(a)=(a^{2}-1)^{2}-0.1a, whose right well is better. We use an exact critic Q=−cQ=-c and Gaussian policies πμ=𝒩⁡(μ,σ2)\pi_{\mu}=\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2}), with fixed σ=0.4\sigma=0.4, τ=0.1\tau=0.1, λ=0.05\lambda=0.05, and T=τ+λT=\tau+\lambda.

Forward fitting changes the update direction. Let ν\nu denote the candidate mean and m∗:=𝔼qμ∗​[a]m_{*}:=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\mu}^{*}}[a]. We differentiate with respect to ν\nu, holding the reference πμ\pi_{\mu} and target qμ∗q_{\mu}^{*} fixed. At ν=μ\nu=\mu, REPPO’s KL regularization is inactive:

∇νLREPPO​(ν)|ν=μ\displaystyle\left.\nabla_{\nu}L_{\mathrm{REPPO}}(\nu)\right|_{\nu=\mu} =T∇νDKL(πν∥qμ∗)|ν=μ=𝔼πμ[c′(a)],\displaystyle=T\left.\nabla_{\nu}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\nu}\|q_{\mu}^{*})\right|_{\nu=\mu}=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\mu}}[c^{\prime}(a)], (10)
∇νLFERPO​(ν,μ)|ν=μ\displaystyle\left.\nabla_{\nu}L_{\mathrm{FERPO}}(\nu;\mu)\right|_{\nu=\mu} =∇νDKL(qμ∗∥πν)|ν=μ=μ−m∗σ2=1λ𝔼qμ∗[c′(a)].\displaystyle=\left.\nabla_{\nu}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_{\mu}^{*}\|\pi_{\nu})\right|_{\nu=\mu}=\frac{\mu-m_{*}}{\sigma^{2}}=\frac{1}{\lambda}\mathbb{E}_{q_{\mu}^{*}}[c^{\prime}(a)].

Both methods average the same cost derivative under different distributions (derivation: Appendix B.5). FERPO’s value-based target can weight distant low-cost regions: at B (μ=−0.6\mu=-0.6), 𝔼πμ​[c′]=0.284\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\mu}}[c^{\prime}]=0.284 and 𝔼qμ∗​[c′]=−0.0419\mathbb{E}_{q_{\mu}^{*}}[c^{\prime}]=-0.0419. Gradient descent moves REPPO left and FERPO right toward m∗≃−0.466m_{*}\simeq-0.466 (Figure 1).

Recovering the direction with SNIS. At B, SNIS with K=1,024K=1{,}024 rollout-policy samples recovers the rightward direction in only 26.4%26.4\% of batches: the better well is rarely sampled. Keeping the target fixed and sampling from rκ=𝒩⁡(μ,κ2​σ2)r_{\kappa}=\mathcal{N}(\mu,\kappa^{2}\sigma^{2}) with proposal-corrected importance weights raises recovery to 98.9%98.9\% for κ=2\kappa=2 and 99.9%99.9\% for κ=3\kappa=3. Appendix A.1 gives the estimator and sampling results (Figure 6).

5.2 Computational cost

We time updates on fixed synthetic rollouts using REPPO’s published configuration (?), including its 16 KL samples per state. Uncached FERPO samples KK actions and evaluates QQ at every actor epoch; cached FERPO reuses actions, rollout log probabilities, and QQ values after critic training, recomputing weights as the multipliers change. Cached actor updates are faster than REPPO for K=4K=4–6464; uncached updates become slower at K≥32K\geq 32 (Figure 2; protocol in Appendix A.2). At K=16K=16, uncached FERPO reduces combined actor-and-critic update time by 6.9% relative to REPPO. Caching provides a further 16.4% reduction, bringing the total saving to 22.2%. A drawback is higher GPU memory usage: on CheetahRun, peak GPU memory usage is 22.4% higher for uncached FERPO and 25.6% higher for cached FERPO than for REPPO, because PyTorch retains additional memory after updates.

5.3 Ablations

Number of SNIS samples. To test whether a larger sampling budget improves learning, we vary the number of rollout-policy action samples per state, K∈{2,4,8,16}K\in\{2,4,8,16\}, on G1 flat terrain with adaptive temperature. Mean return improves as KK increases, with smaller gains at larger sample counts suggesting diminishing returns. At 50.07M environment steps, increasing KK from 8 to 16 raises mean return from 34.32±0.1834.32\pm 0.18 to 34.81±0.2434.81\pm 0.24 (mean ±\pm standard error of the mean, SEM; Figure 3, left), while doubling the number of candidate actions evaluated.

Temperature. To assess the contribution of entropy regularization, we compare adaptive temperature with τ=0\tau=0 at K=16K=16 using the same G1 evaluation budget. Without entropy regularization, mean return falls to 30.32±0.2730.32\pm 0.27 (mean ±\pm SEM; Figure 3, left), 4.49 points below the adaptive control. FERPO’s maximum-entropy formulation therefore achieves higher mean return than the variant without entropy regularization on this task (see Appendix A.3.1 for details).

ESS versus KL control. On HopperHop and AcrobotSwingupSparse, both controllers support learning at suitable settings, with task-dependent best returns. We retain ESS control because it directly regulates SNIS weight concentration and shows lower temporal variation at comparable achieved ESS in these experiments (Appendix A.3.6).

Cached QQ values. To test whether caching speeds up training while retaining performance, we complete critic training before the actor phase, freeze the critic, and cache candidate actions, QQ values, and rollout log probabilities. Actor updates reuse these quantities while recomputing SNIS weights. On G1 with K=8K=8, cached and uncached updates reach 33.58±0.4033.58\pm 0.40 and 34.03±0.2134.03\pm 0.21 at 50.07M steps (mean ±\pm SEM over five seeds; Figure 3, middle). Caching reduces mean time to complete this budget from 68.4 to 55.7 minutes, an 18.6% saving. It therefore trades a modest observed return gap for faster training. Details are provided in Appendix A.3.3.

Cached VV extension. A learned QQ function must approximate both the immediate reward and future returns, and may therefore fail to preserve the reward’s shape across actions. Learning this shape can be particularly difficult in sparse reward settings, where few sampled transitions yield nonzero rewards. To mitigate this source of error, we extend the cached QQ variant above by replacing its critic with a soft state-value function. For each rollout state, we simulate KK candidate actions and, after fitting and freezing VV, cache r⁡(s,a)+γ​V​(s′)r(s,a)+\gamma V(s^{\prime}) as a one-sample Monte Carlo estimate of QV​(s,a)Q_{V}(s,a) for reuse throughout actor updates. This incorporates the observed immediate reward directly, at the cost of KK additional environment calls per rollout state. In massively parallel online RL, these independent one-step simulations can be batched on the GPU (?), and caching amortizes their cost across all actor epochs. With Warp graph execution and batched candidate simulation during rollout, cached VV is only 8.4% slower per training iteration than uncached QQ on AcrobotSwingupSparse with K=16K=16: 8.51 versus 7.85 seconds on an A100, measured after warmup. The KK additional transitions nevertheless increase the total simulation budget by a factor of K+1=17K+1=17. Figure 3 (right) compares returns over 12 seeds. See Appendix A.3.4 for more details.

5.4 Learning benchmarks

We evaluate whether FERPO’s policy updates translate into competitive final performance across three benchmark suites: 22 DeepMind Control Suite (DMC) tasks (?) and four G1/T1 locomotion tasks in MuJoCo Playground (?), and eight ManiSkill manipulation tasks (?). All baseline results come from the experiments accompanying the REPPO paper (?). For each benchmark suite, we train FERPO with exactly the same actor and critic architectures as REPPO. Alongside REPPO, we compare with PPO (?) and PPO (Brax) separately on DMC, PPO on ManiSkill, and FastTD3 (?), a scalable variant of TD3 (?), on DMC. For each of these additional baseline families, we select one configuration per suite using performance at 50M steps and keep that configuration fixed across the suite’s tasks. Appendix A.3 provides the selection protocol and all per-environment learning curves. The G1/T1 FERPO results use K=16K=16 and normalized ESS target 0.650.65, with eight completed seeds per task.

Figure 4 aggregates results separately within each suite using the interquartile mean (IQM). Every environment receives equal total weight, divided equally among its available seeds; returns and success rates retain their original units. We focus the comparison on the final common evaluation budget: 50M interactions for DMC and G1/T1, and 49,971,200 interactions for ManiSkill. Individual IQM uncertainties use pointwise 95% bootstrap confidence intervals from 10,000 seed resamples within environments, matching Figure 4. Below, estimate ±\pm half the bootstrap interval width gives a symmetric approximation; all significance statements use the original interval bounds.

Final performance. On DMC, FERPO reaches an IQM return of 897.7±6.7897.7\pm 6.7. REPPO reaches 891.0±6.4891.0\pm 6.4, FastTD3 890.6±12.8890.6\pm 12.8, PPO (Brax) 542.8±30.2542.8\pm 30.2, and PPO 309.8±9.4309.8\pm 9.4. FERPO therefore has the highest point estimate, with a small numerical lead over REPPO and FastTD3 and a much larger lead over both PPO families. On G1/T1, REPPO reaches 34.63±0.1734.63\pm 0.17, compared with 33.22±0.2833.22\pm 0.28 for FERPO. FERPO’s endpoint estimate is slightly higher on T1 flat and similar on T1 rough, while REPPO leads on both G1 tasks (Figure 14). On ManiSkill, FERPO’s success-rate IQM is (95.67±1.83)%(95.67\pm 1.83)\%; REPPO reaches (95.52±1.85)%(95.52\pm 1.85)\%, and PPO reaches (84.61±9.49)%(84.61\pm 9.49)\%. The two leading ManiSkill point estimates differ by only 0.15 percentage points.

Beyond final performance, FERPO reaches high returns on DMC and high success rates on ManiSkill with fewer environment interactions than REPPO (Figure 4). This sample-efficiency advantage complements its lower optimization cost: at K=16K=16, combined actor-and-critic updates take 6.9% less time in the matched A100 benchmark (Section 5.2). Together, these results suggest improved wall-clock efficiency.

6 Conclusion, limitations, and future work

FERPO performs on-policy maximum-entropy policy improvement by fitting an entropy- and KL-regularized target through forward KL. Critic values weight actions sampled from the rollout policy using self-normalized importance sampling, avoiding critic action derivatives. An ESS controller regulates the concentration of these weights.

On DMC and ManiSkill, FERPO reaches high performance with fewer environment interactions than REPPO and achieves competitive final results. At K=16K=16, combined actor-and-critic update time is 6.9% lower than REPPO for uncached FERPO and we also evaluate cached FERPO with a 22.2% actor update speedup. Ablations on G1 flat terrain highlight the benefit of entropy regularization and gains from larger SNIS candidate sets. Limitations include critic-value errors, finite-sample importance-sampling errors, restricted Gaussian policies, and higher GPU memory use. With eight seeds per task, FERPO remains below REPPO on the G1/T1 suite aggregate at the same environment-interaction budget. The gap is concentrated on the G1 tasks; T1 endpoints are similar or slightly higher for FERPO under the recorded evaluation protocols.

State-value FERPO combines one-step simulation with a learned state-value critic to score candidate actions. Its higher returns on AcrobotSwingupSparse and the modest iteration-time overhead measured for its optimized implementation make it a particularly promising direction for future work. Two further directions are FERPO in discrete action spaces and combining FERPO with diffusion policies. For small discrete action spaces, target normalization and the forward-KL objective could be evaluated by exact summation over actions and larger ones through sampling. Diffusion-augmented MDPs (DA-MDPs) (?) offer a promising and relatively straightforward route to combining FERPO with expressive diffusion policies: FERPO’s forward-KL updates could be applied to individual denoising transitions in the augmented MDP.

A.2 Computation and memory on the A100

A.2.1 Update-cost protocol

The update-cost measurements use one NVIDIA A100-SXM4-40GB with AMD EPYC 7H12 host CPUs, PyTorch 2.9.1+cu128, FP32 parameters, matmul precision medium, and one PyTorch CPU thread, without AMP or compilation. We use the official REPPO PyTorch implementation at commit 05a5776 and the published large-data MuJoCo Playground configuration described in Section 5.2.22 2 Pinned REPPO source; the PyTorch and JAX implementations both use 16 samples for the KL estimate. Each rollout has 131,072 states, with eight epochs of 64 minibatches of 2048. The shared baseline has 17 observation and six action dimensions, a three-layer width-512 actor, and two-layer width-512 critic encoder, Q head, and auxiliary predictor. FERPO evaluates all 2,048​K2{,}048K candidate state-action pairs in each minibatch together.

FERPO completes critic training before its actor phase; REPPO retains its interleaved update schedule. Three warmup minibatches precede each trial. We use seeds 1–3 and randomize method order within each repetition. CUDA events measure actor time; synchronized wall time measures the complete update. Peak allocated PyTorch memory covers the complete update, including rollout tensors and optimizer state, but excludes simulator memory and allocator reservation.

A.2.2 Memory cost

REPPO backpropagates through Q for one action per state; its 16 KL samples require policy evaluations only. FERPO instead evaluates many actions together through Q. Even without retaining a backward graph, these larger batches require larger temporary tensors. FERPO’s peak allocated memory therefore increases with KK (Figure 2).

Cached FERPO additionally stores KK actions, reference log probabilities, and Q values for each of SS rollout states. With action dimension dd and FP32 storage, this requires

Mcache=4​S​K​(d+2)​bytes.M_{\mathrm{cache}}=4SK(d+2)\ \text{bytes}. (12)

For the measured rollout size at K=16K=16, the cache occupies 64 MiB for d=6d=6 and 528 MiB for d=64d=64.

A.2.3 Memory across rollout and update phases

We separately profile CheetahRun with the same network and rollout configuration at K=16K=16. The matched comparison uses seeds 2 and 3 on one A100 node, with a fresh process per method and seed, two warmup iterations, and three measured iterations. The simulator and a 32-environment evaluation instance remain resident; initialization and evaluation are excluded from the measurement windows. NVML samples total process memory every 5 ms, including runtime and allocator reservations; these sampled peaks are lower bounds. PyTorch records allocated and reserved peaks separately for each phase. We exclude seed 1 from this comparison because uncached FERPO ran on a second A100 with a different driver.

All three methods reach their process peak during rollouts (Table 2). Active PyTorch rollout allocations are nearly equal, while larger pools remain reserved after FERPO’s updates. These process footprints therefore reflect allocator retention as well as live tensors, rather than minimum GPU capacity requirements.

A.3 Learning ablations and benchmarks

A.3.1 Ablation details

The candidate-count ablation uses per-seed G1JoystickFlatTerrain evaluation logs for K=2,4,8,16K=2,4,8,16. All four settings use actor/critic and temperature learning rates of 0.00030.0003, entropy target factor −0.5-0.5, and normalized ESS target 0.850.85. The replacements correct the historical K=2K=2 entropy target of −1.0-1.0 and K=16K=16 temperature learning rate of 0.0030.003; those superseded observations are excluded from the plots. We report arithmetic means with one-SEM error bars and bands. The temperature comparison reuses the corrected K=16K=16 control. These ablation cohorts remain separate from the G1/T1 benchmark cohort below, which uses normalized ESS target 0.650.65.

The candidate-count plot in Figure 3 (left) uses the final common evaluation at 50,069,504 environment steps, rather than selecting a best checkpoint or averaging a trailing window. There are eight seeds at this endpoint for K=2,16K=2,16, ten for K=4,8K=4,8, and eight for the additional τ=0\tau=0 marker at K=16K=16. The no-entropy learning curve in Figure 7 uses the same eight completed seeds at every evaluation. The corrected adaptive-temperature control uses seeds 1–8. Both temperature curves and all candidate-count endpoints show mean ±\pm one SEM. All eight no-entropy runs reach 50,069,504 steps, with final mean 30.32±0.2730.32\pm 0.27. They disable entropy regularization and its temperature update. The entropy target changed from −1.0-1.0 in the historical runs to −0.5-0.5 in the new runs, but is inactive when τ=0\tau=0. For all G1 ablations, including cached-Q and critic-width comparisons, we compute SEM=s/n\mathrm{SEM}=s/\sqrt{n}, where ss is the sample standard deviation (with n−1n-1 in its variance denominator) and nn is the number of contributing seeds. These are standard errors of the mean, not 95% confidence intervals. Benchmark curves use IQM and bootstrap intervals as specified below.

A.3.2 Critic-width protocol

The width comparison uses the uploaded G1 preset on G1JoystickFlatTerrain with learning rate 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}, target entropy factor −0.5-0.5, eight critic epochs, HL-Gauss loss, and auxiliary weight one. Both methods use the full rollout. FERPO uses K=8K=8; REPPO retains its pathwise actor update and KL bound 0.1. We vary hidden width in the critic encoder, QQ head, and auxiliary predictor together; depth and the 512-wide actor are fixed. Each endpoint is the final deterministic evaluation at 50,069,504 rollout interactions. Seeds 1–2 contribute at each width except REPPO width 1,024, for which only seed 1 is available. These are dedicated critic-width runs, separate from the published REPPO benchmark results. We have not measured action-gradient approximation error in these runs.

At 50.07M interactions, reducing critic width from 124 to 62 lowers FERPO’s mean return from 23.04 to 6.29 and REPPO’s from 22.12 to 4.19. Both methods therefore rely on sufficient critic capacity.

A.3.3 Cached-Q timing protocol and elapsed-time curves

We compare interleaved critic/actor updates with a staged variant that first fits the critic, then freezes it and caches K=8K=8 actions, their QQ values, and rollout log probabilities. Actor training recomputes SNIS weights as the multipliers change. Both methods use eight full-rollout critic epochs, 1,024-wide critics, learning rate 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}, and target entropy factor −0.5-0.5. The five-seed rollout curves are unsmoothed. Final mean returns at 50,069,504 steps are 34.03±0.2134.03\pm 0.21 uncached and 33.58±0.4033.58\pm 0.40 cached (mean ±\pm SEM).

The timing annotation in Figure 3 (middle) and elapsed-time curves in Figure 9 use seeds 3–5 for each method. These six runs shared the same Vega allocation and node, with one NVIDIA A100-SXM4-40GB and a separate CPU set per run. Seeds 1–2 remain in the five-seed rollout comparison in Figure 3 (middle), but are excluded from timing because their cached and uncached runs used different clusters. The per-run clock starts before environment construction and includes simulation, learning, evaluation, and checkpointing; scheduler waiting time is excluded. Mean completion times at 50,069,504 rollout steps are 55.7 minutes cached and 68.4 minutes uncached. The time reduction is 1−Tcached/Tuncached=18.6%1-T_{\mathrm{cached}}/T_{\mathrm{uncached}}=18.6\%; the throughput increase is Tuncached/Tcached−1=22.9%T_{\mathrm{uncached}}/T_{\mathrm{cached}}-1=22.9\%. These are measured runtimes for this allocation.

We use recorded evaluation timestamps for the time curves. Within each method, we linearly interpolate each seed’s return to common elapsed times, then compute the mean and SEM over all three seeds. The bold mean curve ends when the first run in that method finishes; faint individual curves continue to their own final evaluation. We do not extrapolate or carry completed returns forward. The arrow separately marks the mean completion times from the run summaries, including the final checkpoint. The five-seed curves in Figure 3 (middle) use recorded rollout-step coordinates directly, without interpolation.

A.3.4 State-value critic with candidate simulation

We compare standard uncached FERPO with its cached VV extension on AcrobotSwingupSparse. For a fixed fitted critic, the ideal candidate score is QV(s,a)=r(s,a)+γ𝔼s′∼P(⋅∣s,a)[Vψ(s′)]Q_{V}(s,a)=r(s,a)+\gamma\mathbb{E}_{s^{\prime}\sim P(\cdot\mid s,a)}[V_{\psi}(s^{\prime})]. We approximate the transition expectation with one simulated successor per candidate, giving Q^V​(s,a)=r⁡(s,a)+γ​Vψ​(s′)\widehat{Q}_{V}(s,a)=r(s,a)+\gamma V_{\psi}(s^{\prime}). This incorporates the observed immediate reward directly while using a one-sample Monte Carlo estimate of the future value. Scores are computed after fitting VψV_{\psi} and held fixed throughout actor training. The bootstrap is zero at true terminals; time limits retain the value of the final observation.

Both methods use K=16K=16, 512-wide critics, eight critic epochs, HL-Gauss loss, auxiliary weight one, learning rate 10−310^{-3}, and target entropy factor −1-1. Across 12 matched seed identifiers, cached VV reaches 324.79±75.28324.79\pm 75.28 at 59.90 million rollout steps, compared with 99.46±110.7599.46\pm 110.75 for uncached QQ (mean ±\pm one SD; Figure 3, right). The deterministic evaluation curves are unsmoothed. Each rollout step requires KK additional candidate transitions, so cached VV uses 1717 times as many simulator transitions at this rollout budget.

Efficient candidate simulation. We combine Warp graph execution with parallel simulation of all KK candidates across environments. Candidates are sampled and simulated during rollout, branching from each state without altering the rollout trajectory. Their rewards and next observations remain on the GPU until the critic has been fitted, then serve to construct the score cache. This avoids repeated transfers of simulator states between CPU and GPU. Actor epochs reuse the candidates and scores while updating their SNIS weights. Since observation normalization can change during rollout, we retain the sampling densities and correct these weights for any difference from the frozen rollout reference.

Timing protocol. We benchmark both methods on the same NVIDIA A100-SXM4-40GB with Warp graphs enabled. Both use 1,024 environments, 128 rollout steps per iteration, actor and critic widths of 512, eight actor and critic epochs, 64 minibatches, and one PyTorch CPU thread. We run three repetitions in separate processes, randomizing method order and averaging five iterations after two warmup iterations. GPU synchronization at iteration boundaries ensures that timings include all simulation and learning work; startup, compilation warmup, evaluation, external logging, and checkpointing are excluded. Cached VV takes 8.508 seconds per iteration versus 7.846 seconds for uncached QQ, an 8.4% overhead.

A.3.5 Additional planned ablation

The following additional G1 comparison remains planned. It will use matched seeds, interaction budgets, and evaluation protocols, keeping other settings fixed.

Forward KL instead of ESS regularization. We will replace the log-ESS constraint with 𝔼s∼droll[DKL(πroll(⋅∣s)∥πθ(⋅∣s))]≤0.1\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\mathrm{roll}}}[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(\cdot\mid s)\|\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s))]\leq 0.1, matching REPPO’s bound. The action expectation in this forward KL is under the old rollout policy. We will adapt λ\lambda using the KL constraint gap and compare return, achieved KL, and normalized ESS against the ESS-controlled baseline.

A.3.6 ESS versus policy-KL control

We compare log-ESS control (Eq. 8) at etarget∈{0.40,0.50,0.65,0.85}e_{\mathrm{target}}\in\{0.40,0.50,0.65,0.85\} with control of the rollout-state mean DKL(πroll∥πcurr)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}\|\pi_{\mathrm{curr}}) at ϵ∈{0.03,0.10,0.20,0.30}\epsilon\in\{0.03,0.10,0.20,0.30\} nats. Both adapt λ\lambda with the same forward-KL actor objective. ESS controls SNIS weight concentration; policy KL measures policy displacement.

We use uncached FERPO (K=16K=16) on HopperHop and AcrobotSwingupSparse with 12 seeds per setting. All runs use width-512 critics, eight epochs, 64 minibatches, HL-Gauss loss, auxiliary weight one, actor/critic and temperature learning rates 10−310^{-3}, and entropy target factor −1-1. Rollouts comprise 1,024 environments and 128 steps. Final returns average the first episode from each of 128 deterministic evaluation environments, with frozen normalizers and fixed initial states within each run.

Both controllers support learning at suitable settings, with task-dependent preferred regularization strengths and no consistent return advantage for either controller (Figure 10).

Direct ESS control generally tracks its target, whereas fixed policy-KL bounds produce ESS that varies across tasks and training (Figure 11). At comparable mean achieved ESS, direct control shows less temporal variation, although the aggressive ESS target 0.400.40 remains variable on Acrobot. These observations motivate ESS as a direct, interpretable control of sampling-weight concentration.

A.3.7 Data and comparison protocol

The benchmark comprises 22 DMC, four G1/T1, and eight ManiSkill tasks. FERPO uses training-log return evaluations for 19 DMC tasks and success rates for ManiSkill. The three Walker tasks use separate policy-evaluation CSVs, whose task metadata and reconstructed means and counts match the original benchmark summaries. Walker has ten evaluated seeds per task beyond 50M steps, replacing the older partial training-log evaluations. For Walker, we display the available positive checkpoint evaluations from 3,014,656 through 50,987,008 interactions; seeds 11–12 have no exported evaluation curves and are not counted. The other 19 DMC tasks retain their own recorded evaluation schedules. These existing evaluations use deterministic actions and report 1,000-step episode lengths, but sampling settings differ: the older training evaluator uses 1,024 environments, the newer one uses 128, and the Walker checkpoint evaluator uses 128 episodes. Initial evaluation states are fixed within a run rather than refreshed at every checkpoint. Thus these are existing evaluation exports, not a reevaluation under one identical sampling protocol. The G1/T1 benchmark uses the completed K=16K=16, normalized ESS target 0.650.65 runs, with seeds 1–8 for each task. Actor/critic and temperature learning rates are 0.00030.0003, and the entropy target factor is −0.5-0.5. We use all 21 recorded deterministic training evaluations through 50,069,504 interactions, averaging the first episode from each of 128 parallel environments. The ManiSkill source label “FEPPO architecture” denotes FERPO. We retain all available evaluated seeds within their observed ranges, so counts may vary across checkpoints; training-only runs contribute no observations. Each DMC panel labels the number of contributing seeds for every method; a range indicates changing availability along the displayed curve. We retain the common 50M budget for numerical method comparisons and do not extrapolate baselines to the last Walker checkpoint.

Baseline sources and configuration selection. All baseline results are drawn from the experiments accompanying the REPPO paper (?). REPPO uses the official per-task trial CSVs at commit 05a5776.33 3 Official REPPO result CSVs at the pinned commit. We neither rescale their training horizons nor combine the two PPO families. For the remaining methods, we compare configurations separately by method family and suite (DMC, G1/T1, or ManiSkill). Statistics and display. All benchmark methods show IQM over the available independent seeds. We compute IQM by integrating the middle 50% of empirical probability mass, including fractional observations at quartile boundaries. A.3.8 Pairwise comparisons of final benchmark performance

The endpoint comparison uses the same tasks, available seeds, configuration choices, and weighting as Figure 4. All methods within a suite are compared at its final common budget: 50,000,000 steps for DMC and G1/T1, and 49,971,200 steps for ManiSkill. Each seed contributes its linearly interpolated evaluation score only when that budget lies within its observed range. Individual IQMs and their marginal 95% intervals in Section 5.4 are the existing 10,000-resample Figure 4 estimates.

For the pairwise analysis, we independently resample seeds with replacement within each fixed environment and method, preserving each environment’s seed count and total weight. Numerical seed labels do not establish paired runs across methods, so we do not use a paired-method bootstrap. For each of 100,000 resamples, we compute the suite IQM for each method and subtract the two IQMs of interest. We retain the environment set rather than resampling environments. The procedure uses deterministic method-specific random seeds and reproduces the plotted endpoint IQMs before computing differences.

There are fourteen comparisons: ten on DMC, one on G1/T1, and three on ManiSkill. We use quantiles 0.025/140.025/14 and 1−0.025/141-0.025/14 of each bootstrap difference distribution. These are approximately 99.643% per-comparison intervals, corresponding to a Bonferroni correction that targets at least 95% coverage for the family of fourteen comparisons, subject to the bootstrap approximation. A difference interval entirely above zero supports higher IQM for method A; an interval entirely below zero supports method B. An interval spanning zero is inconclusive and does not establish equal performance. The intervals condition on the observed seeds and selected configurations; they do not account for configuration search or informative missingness.

A.3.9 DMC tasks

A.3.10 G1/T1 locomotion and ManiSkill manipulation

At 50M interactions, FERPO’s IQM returns are 35.56 and 30.38 on G1 flat and rough terrain, compared with REPPO’s 37.60 and 32.89. On T1 flat and rough terrain, FERPO reaches 37.05 and 30.68, compared with REPPO’s 36.48 and 30.73. Thus FERPO has a slightly higher point estimate on T1 flat and a similar endpoint on T1 rough, while REPPO retains a larger lead on both G1 tasks.

A.4 FERPO pseudocode

Algorithm 1 shows the interleaved critic and actor updates used in the main learning setup. Critic targets are computed once per rollout; candidate actions and their Q values are refreshed for each actor update. We write ⟨⋅⟩ℬ\langle\cdot\rangle_{\mathcal{B}} for a minibatch average and sg\operatorname{sg} for stop-gradient. Bootstrap states use the final observation before any environment reset. The frozen parameters ϕ¯\bar{\phi} are a snapshot for target construction.

ℒHL​-​Gauss\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{HL\text{-}Gauss}} matches the critic’s categorical prediction to a Gaussian-smoothed histogram of the scalar target GtG_{t}; Qϕ​(s,a)Q_{\phi}(s,a) is the mean of this prediction. ℒaux\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{aux}} predicts the next critic representation and reward, with fixed targets and zero loss at episode ends (Section 3.3). The target recursion adds the next action’s entropy contribution once, outside the TD mixture. Actor updates differentiate only policy log probabilities and multiplier losses; their gradients do not change the critic or rollout policy.

Policy parameterization and action bounds. For bounded-action environments, we use a tanh-squashed Gaussian policy πθ\pi_{\theta}, following REPPO (?) and SAC (?): z∼𝒩⁡(μθ​(s),diag⁡(σθ2​(s)))z\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{\theta}(s),\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_{\theta}^{2}(s))), a=tanh⁡(z)a=\tanh(z), where a neural network parameterizes μθ\mu_{\theta} and σθ\sigma_{\theta}. Actions are rescaled to the environment’s action bounds where needed. Policy log densities include the corresponding change-of-variables correction.

For cached FERPO, complete critic training first, freeze QϕQ_{\phi}, and sample and store ai​(s)a_{i}(s), vi​(s)v_{i}(s), and bi​(s)b_{i}(s) once for every rollout state. Reuse these tensors throughout actor training, recomputing ℓi​(s)\ell_{i}(s) and wi​(s)w_{i}(s) as τ\tau and λ\lambda change; release the cache before the next rollout. Appendix A.2 reports the runtime and memory costs of this schedule.

A.5 State-dependent normalization in policy fitting

AWR’s practical regression objective omits the per-state normalizer (?, Eqs. 8–10); AWAC explicitly discusses the same omission (?, Appendix A-B). To isolate its effect, fix a state distribution dd, the rollout policy πroll(⋅∣s)\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(\cdot\mid s), advantage estimates A⁡(s,a)A(s,a), and λ>0\lambda>0. We consider the exponential weights before clipping and assume the expectations and gradients below exist. Define

u⁡(s,a)\displaystyle u(s,a) :=exp⁡(A⁡(s,a)/λ),\displaystyle:=\exp(A(s,a)/\lambda), Z⁡(s)\displaystyle Z(s) :=𝔼a∼πroll(⋅∣s)[u(s,a)],\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(\cdot\mid s)}[u(s,a)], (13)
qA​(a∣s)\displaystyle q_{A}(a\mid s) :=πroll​(a∣s)​u​(s,a)Z⁡(s),\displaystyle:=\frac{\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(a\mid s)u(s,a)}{Z(s)}, 0\displaystyle 0 <Z⁡(s)<∞.\displaystyle<Z(s)<\infty.

Let ℓθ(s):=−𝔼a∼qA(⋅∣s)[logπθ(a∣s)]\ell_{\theta}(s):=-\mathbb{E}_{a\sim q_{A}(\cdot\mid s)}[\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)]. The normalized forward-KL fit minimizes Lnorm​(θ):=𝔼s∼d​[ℓθ​(s)]L_{\mathrm{norm}}(\theta):=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d}[\ell_{\theta}(s)], up to a constant independent of θ\theta. Omitting Z⁡(s)Z(s) instead gives

Lomit​(θ)\displaystyle L_{\mathrm{omit}}(\theta) :=−𝔼s∼d𝔼a∼πroll(⋅∣s)[u(s,a)logπθ(a∣s)]\displaystyle:=-\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d}\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(\cdot\mid s)}[u(s,a)\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)] (14)
=𝔼s∼d​[Z⁡(s)​ℓθ​(s)].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d}[Z(s)\ell_{\theta}(s)].

Thus, holding the target weights fixed during actor fitting and writing gθ​(s):=∇θℓθ​(s)g_{\theta}(s):=\nabla_{\theta}\ell_{\theta}(s),

∇θLnorm=𝔼s∼d​[gθ​(s)],∇θLomit=𝔼s∼d​[Z⁡(s)​gθ​(s)].\nabla_{\theta}L_{\mathrm{norm}}=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d}[g_{\theta}(s)],\qquad\nabla_{\theta}L_{\mathrm{omit}}=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d}[Z(s)g_{\theta}(s)]. (15)

The omission therefore changes the relative influence of states even with unlimited data. A constant Z⁡(s)Z(s) only rescales the gradient. With independent, unrestricted fitting at each state, both objectives recover qAq_{A}. With a shared neural policy, varying Z⁡(s)Z(s) can change the overall gradient direction and, when the target cannot be fitted exactly, the optimal approximation. The size of this effect depends on the variation in Z⁡(s)Z(s) and the alignment of gradients across states.

An advantage baseline does not generally remove this reweighting: for A⁡(s,a)=Q⁡(s,a)−V⁡(s)A(s,a)=Q(s,a)-V(s), Z(s)=e−V(s)/λ𝔼a∼πroll(⋅∣s)[eQ⁡(s,a)/λ]Z(s)=e^{-V(s)/\lambda}\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(\cdot\mid s)}[e^{Q(s,a)/\lambda}], which need not equal one. The baseline cancels from qAq_{A} after normalization, but affects state weights when Z⁡(s)Z(s) is omitted. AWR’s additional weight clipping changes the action weights as well (?, Section 3.3).

FERPO estimates normalized weights separately within each state using Eq. 6. SNIS has finite-sample bias but is consistent under the usual integrability and sampling assumptions (?, Section 9.2); see also Appendix B.5.2. This establishes a difference in the fitted objective, rather than a general performance ordering.

B.3.1 From target ESS to policy total variation

A decrease in the population forward-KL fitting loss suffices to transfer the target’s divergence control to the actor in total variation. We use the half-L1L^{1} convention in Section 2 and natural logarithms throughout.

We restate the actor-control assumption of Proposition 1. Fix a state and a target q∗q^{*}, suppressing state conditioning. Assume q∗≪πrollq^{*}\ll\pi_{\mathrm{roll}} and 𝔼πroll​[(q∗/πroll)2]<∞\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}}[(q^{*}/\pi_{\mathrm{roll}})^{2}]<\infty, and let e∞:=1/𝔼πroll​[(q∗/πroll)2]e_{\infty}:=1/\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}}[(q^{*}/\pi_{\mathrm{roll}})^{2}]. Suppose the actor update does not increase the population forward-KL fitting objective:

DKL(q∗∥πcurr)≤DKL(q∗∥πroll).D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q^{*}\|\pi_{\mathrm{curr}})\leq D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q^{*}\|\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}). (24)

Then Eq. 9 holds:

12​DTV​(πcurr,πroll)2\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}D_{\mathrm{TV}}(\pi_{\mathrm{curr}},\pi_{\mathrm{roll}})^{2} ≤DKL(q∗∥πroll)\displaystyle\leq D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q^{*}\|\pi_{\mathrm{roll}})
≤D2(q∗∥πroll)=−loge∞.\displaystyle\leq D_{2}(q^{*}\|\pi_{\mathrm{roll}})=-\log e_{\infty}.

No exact minimization or Gaussian policy assumption is required.

Proof of the actor-TV bound in Proposition 1.

The triangle inequality, obtained by adding and subtracting q∗q^{*} inside the absolute value in the TV definition, gives

DTV​(πcurr,πroll)≤DTV​(πcurr,q∗)+DTV​(q∗,πroll).D_{\mathrm{TV}}(\pi_{\mathrm{curr}},\pi_{\mathrm{roll}})\leq D_{\mathrm{TV}}(\pi_{\mathrm{curr}},q^{*})+D_{\mathrm{TV}}(q^{*},\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}).

TV is symmetric, so Pinsker’s inequality (?, Theorem 31) can bound both terms using KL divergences with q∗q^{*} as their first argument. Applying Eq. 24 then yields

DTV​(πcurr,πroll)\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{TV}}(\pi_{\mathrm{curr}},\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}) ≤12DKL(q∗∥πcurr)+12DKL(q∗∥πroll)\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{2}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q^{*}\|\pi_{\mathrm{curr}})}+\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{2}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q^{*}\|\pi_{\mathrm{roll}})}
≤2​12DKL(q∗∥πroll)=2DKL(q∗∥πroll).\displaystyle\leq 2\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{2}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q^{*}\|\pi_{\mathrm{roll}})}=\sqrt{2D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q^{*}\|\pi_{\mathrm{roll}})}.
