DKL(q∗∥πcurr)−DKL(q∗∥πroll)=−𝔼q∗[logπcurrπroll].D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q^{*}\|\pi_{\mathrm{curr}})-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q^{*}\|\pi_{\mathrm{roll}})=-\mathbb{E}_{q^{*}}\!\left[\log\frac{\pi_{\mathrm{curr}}}{\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}}\right].

Thus Eq. 24 requires only that the actor increase or preserve the target-weighted population log likelihood. This is the objective approximated by the SNIS actor loss; it is distinct from an assumption of higher environment return.

Averaging over rollout states. The result also holds on average without per-state fitting improvement. All distributions below are conditioned on ss. Squaring the first Pinsker bound above and using (x+y)2≤2​(x+y)(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y})^{2}\leq 2(x+y) gives the pointwise inequality

DTV(πcurr,πroll)2≤DKL(q∗∥πcurr)+DKL(q∗∥πroll).D_{\mathrm{TV}}(\pi_{\mathrm{curr}},\pi_{\mathrm{roll}})^{2}\leq D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q^{*}\|\pi_{\mathrm{curr}})+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q^{*}\|\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}).

Assume the relevant expectations are finite and that

𝔼s∼droll[DKL(q∗∥πcurr)]≤𝔼s∼droll[DKL(q∗∥πroll)].\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\mathrm{roll}}}[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q^{*}\|\pi_{\mathrm{curr}})]\leq\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\mathrm{roll}}}[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q^{*}\|\pi_{\mathrm{roll}})].

Averaging the pointwise inequality and applying the target-divergence bound in Eq. 9 yields

12​𝔼s∼droll​[DTV​(πcurr,πroll)2]\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\mathrm{roll}}}[D_{\mathrm{TV}}(\pi_{\mathrm{curr}},\pi_{\mathrm{roll}})^{2}] ≤𝔼s∼droll[DKL(q∗∥πroll)]\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\mathrm{roll}}}[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q^{*}\|\pi_{\mathrm{roll}})]
≤−𝔼s∼droll​[log⁡e∞​(s)].\displaystyle\leq-\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\mathrm{roll}}}[\log e_{\infty}(s)].

If the geometric mean of population ESS meets the controller target, 𝔼s∼droll​[log⁡e∞​(s)]≥log⁡etarget\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\mathrm{roll}}}[\log e_{\infty}(s)]\geq\log e_{\mathrm{target}}, the right-hand side is at most −log⁡etarget-\log e_{\mathrm{target}}. This controls average squared TV, rather than the largest deviation across states. Decreases in finite-sample SNIS loss and empirical ESS control do not by themselves guarantee these population conditions. Nor does the TV bound imply an upper bound on the fitted actor’s KL; it cannot replace the KL penalty in Eq. 3 without further assumptions.

B.4 Convergence under exact fitting

The regularized target in Eq. 5 interpolates between the reference policy and the Boltzmann distribution. Repeated exact updates reach the Boltzmann distribution when the reference is replaced by the fitted policy after every update. The following result quantifies how λ\lambda controls this convergence for a fixed critic.

Proposition 2 (Convergence of exact FERPO updates for a fixed critic).

Fix a state ss, a critic Q⁡(s,⋅)Q(s,\cdot), and a temperature τ>0\tau>0. Suppress state conditioning and let p⁡(a):=exp⁡(Q⁡(s,a)/τ)/Z⁡(s)p(a):=\exp(Q(s,a)/\tau)/Z(s) be normalizable. Assume DKL(p∥π0)<∞D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|\pi_{0})<\infty and fix 0<λ<∞0<\lambda<\infty. At each iteration, compute the unrestricted target and fit it exactly:

qn∗:=arg​minq{τDKL(q∥p)+λDKL(q∥πn)},πn+1=qn∗.q_{n}^{*}:=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{q}\left\{\tau D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p)+\lambda D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|\pi_{n})\right\},\qquad\pi_{n+1}=q_{n}^{*}.

The policy after n≥1n\geq 1 exact updates is

πn​(a)=1Zn​(s)​π0​(a)(λτ+λ)n​exp⁡[1−(λτ+λ)nτ​Q​(s,a)],\pi_{n}(a)=\frac{1}{Z_{n}(s)}\pi_{0}(a)^{\left(\frac{\lambda}{\tau+\lambda}\right)^{n}}\exp\!\left[\frac{1-\left(\frac{\lambda}{\tau+\lambda}\right)^{n}}{\tau}Q(s,a)\right], (25)

where Zn​(s)Z_{n}(s) normalizes the density. Since (λ/(τ+λ))n→0\left(\lambda/(\tau+\lambda)\right)^{n}\to 0 as n→∞n\to\infty, the initial policy’s exponent vanishes and the coefficient of Q⁡(s,a)Q(s,a) approaches 1/τ1/\tau. Consequently,

limn→∞πn​(a)=exp⁡(Q⁡(s,a)/τ)∫𝒜exp⁡(Q⁡(s,b)/τ)​𝑑b=p⁡(a)almost everywhere,\lim_{n\to\infty}\pi_{n}(a)=\frac{\exp(Q(s,a)/\tau)}{\int_{\mathcal{A}}\exp(Q(s,b)/\tau)\,\mathrm{d}b}=p(a)\quad\text{almost everywhere},

and convergence also holds in total variation. The limit is the unique maximizer of 𝔼a∼q​[Q⁡(s,a)−τ​log⁡q⁡(a)]\mathbb{E}_{a\sim q}[Q(s,a)-\tau\log q(a)], independently of the fixed finite value of λ\lambda. For λ=0\lambda=0, the target is reached in one exact update.

The role of λ\lambda. Equation 25 separates the influence of the initial policy from the Boltzmann target. Larger λ\lambda makes λ/(τ+λ)\lambda/(\tau+\lambda) closer to one, so the initial policy’s influence decays more slowly. Smaller λ\lambda gives faster progress toward the same target. Thus, λ\lambda controls the rate of approach, while τ\tau determines the limiting Boltzmann distribution.

The proposition assumes exact forward-KL fits and a refreshed reference policy at every iteration. Repeated fitting to a single frozen target only recovers that target. It establishes convergence to the Boltzmann distribution of the fixed critic; convergence of full RL training, where the critic is re-estimated, requires a separate policy-iteration argument.

Proof of Proposition 2.

Write β:=λ/(τ+λ)∈(0,1)\beta:=\lambda/(\tau+\lambda)\in(0,1). Equation 5 gives πn+1=p1−β​πnβ/Cn\pi_{n+1}=p^{1-\beta}\pi_{n}^{\beta}/C_{n}, where Cn:=∫p1−β​πnβ​𝑑aC_{n}:=\int p^{1-\beta}\pi_{n}^{\beta}\,\mathrm{d}a. Induction gives πn∝p1−βn​π0βn\pi_{n}\propto p^{1-\beta^{n}}\pi_{0}^{\beta^{n}}. Substituting p∝exp⁡(Q/τ)p\propto\exp(Q/\tau) and β=λ/(τ+λ)\beta=\lambda/(\tau+\lambda) yields Eq. 25. The finite-KL assumption ensures that π0\pi_{0} covers the support of pp; this property is preserved by the update. As n→∞n\to\infty, p1−βn​π0βn→pp^{1-\beta^{n}}\pi_{0}^{\beta^{n}}\to p almost everywhere. The bound p1−t​π0t≤p+π0p^{1-t}\pi_{0}^{t}\leq p+\pi_{0} for 0<t<10<t<1 permits dominated convergence, so the normalizing integral of this geometric mixture tends to one. This proves the stated almost-everywhere limit.

To quantify convergence, Hölder’s inequality and normalization imply 0<Cn≤10<C_{n}\leq 1. Therefore,

DKL(p∥πn+1)=βDKL(p∥πn)+logCn≤βDKL(p∥πn).D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|\pi_{n+1})=\beta D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|\pi_{n})+\log C_{n}\leq\beta D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|\pi_{n}). (26)

Iterating gives the KL contraction bound

DKL(p∥πn+1)≤βDKL(p∥πn),DKL(p∥πn)≤βnDKL(p∥π0).D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|\pi_{n+1})\leq\beta D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|\pi_{n}),\qquad D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|\pi_{n})\leq\beta^{n}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|\pi_{0}). (27)

Pinsker’s inequality then implies convergence in total variation. Optimality of pp follows from Eq. 18. For λ=0\lambda=0, the update minimizes DKL(q∥p)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p) and reaches pp immediately. ∎

Finite-step accuracy and varying multipliers. If D0:=DKL(p∥π0)>ε>0D_{0}:=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|\pi_{0})>\varepsilon>0, then n≥⌈log⁡(D0/ε)/log⁡(1+τ/λ)⌉n\geq\lceil\log(D_{0}/\varepsilon)/\log(1+\tau/\lambda)\rceil exact updates suffice for DKL(p∥πn)≤εD_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|\pi_{n})\leq\varepsilon. For varying coefficients λk>0\lambda_{k}>0 at fixed QQ and τ\tau, βn\beta^{n} is replaced by ∏k=0n−1λk/(τ+λk)\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\lambda_{k}/(\tau+\lambda_{k}); convergence follows if this product tends to zero, as it does for uniformly bounded λk\lambda_{k}.

B.5 Update directions and importance sampling

For a Gaussian policy with fixed covariance, both REPPO and FERPO have mean gradients that can be expressed as averages of cost gradients. REPPO averages under the current policy; FERPO averages under its cost-reweighted target, with a factor 1/λ1/\lambda. We derive these identities and explain how the different distributions produce the opposing directions in Figure 1. We then show why recovering the target direction from samples requires adequate proposal coverage.

B.5.1 Cost gradients under the policy and the target

Fix a state and a cost c⁡(a)=−Qϕ​(s,a)c(a)=-Q_{\phi}(s,a) on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Let πm=𝒩⁡(m,Σ)\pi_{m}=\mathcal{N}(m,\Sigma) be the reference and initial actor, with fixed covariance Σ≻0\Sigma\succ 0. The candidate actor is πn=𝒩⁡(n,Σ)\pi_{n}=\mathcal{N}(n,\Sigma). Fix τ,λ>0\tau,\lambda>0 and write T=τ+λT=\tau+\lambda. FERPO constructs

qm∗(a)=1Zme−c(a)/Tπm(a)λ/T,q_{m}^{*}(a)=\frac{1}{Z_{m}}e^{-c(a)/T}\pi_{m}(a)^{\lambda/T}, (28)

and holds qm∗q_{m}^{*} fixed while fitting πn\pi_{n}. Let m∗​(m):=𝔼a∼qm∗​[a]m^{*}(m):=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim q_{m}^{*}}[a] denote the target mean. Assume cc is continuously differentiable and bounded below, and that cc and ∇c\nabla c grow at most polynomially. These conditions ensure finite target moments and justify the differentiation below.

Proposition 3 (Initial mean-descent directions).

At n=mn=m, REPPO’s KL regularization is inactive. Its mean loss is LR​(n)=𝔼πn​[c]−τ​H​(πn)L_{\mathrm{R}}(n)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{n}}[c]-\tau H(\pi_{n}), while FERPO fits LF(n;m)=DKL(qm∗∥πn)L_{\mathrm{F}}(n;m)=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_{m}^{*}\|\pi_{n}). Their negative gradients are

dR​(m)\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{R}}(m) :=−∇nLR​(n)|n=m=−𝔼a∼πm​[∇c​(a)],\displaystyle:=-\left.\nabla_{n}L_{\mathrm{R}}(n)\right|_{n=m}=-\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{m}}[\nabla c(a)], (29)
dF​(m)\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{F}}(m) :=−∇nLF​(n,m)|n=m=Σ−1​(m∗​(m)−m)=−1λ​𝔼a∼qm∗​[∇c​(a)].\displaystyle:=-\left.\nabla_{n}L_{\mathrm{F}}(n;m)\right|_{n=m}=\Sigma^{-1}\bigl(m^{*}(m)-m\bigr)=-\frac{1}{\lambda}\mathbb{E}_{a\sim q_{m}^{*}}[\nabla c(a)].

The exact forward-KL mean fit sets n=m∗​(m)n=m^{*}(m). Reverse KL to the same frozen target has the same initial descent direction as REPPO, with its negative gradient equal to dR​(m)/Td_{\mathrm{R}}(m)/T.

Proof.

Using the reparameterization a=n+Σ1/2​za=n+\Sigma^{1/2}z, where z∼𝒩⁡(0,I)z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I), we obtain

∇n𝔼a∼πn​[c⁡(a)]=𝔼a∼πn​[∇ac​(a)].\nabla_{n}\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{n}}[c(a)]=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{n}}[\nabla_{a}c(a)].

Since the covariance is fixed, the entropy does not depend on nn. This gives REPPO’s mean-descent direction. For FERPO, expansion of the Gaussian log density gives

LF​(n,m)=12​(n−m∗​(m))⊤​Σ−1​(n−m∗​(m))+const⁡(m).L_{\mathrm{F}}(n;m)=\frac{1}{2}\bigl(n-m^{*}(m)\bigr)^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\bigl(n-m^{*}(m)\bigr)+\mathrm{const}(m). (30)

Differentiating with respect to nn gives the FERPO gradient, and the quadratic is minimized at n=m∗​(m)n=m^{*}(m).

To express FERPO’s gradient in terms of cost gradients, differentiate the target log density with respect to the action:

∇a​log​qm∗​(a)=−1T​(∇c​(a)+λ​Σ−1​(a−m)).\nabla_{a}\log q_{m}^{*}(a)=-\frac{1}{T}\bigl(\nabla c(a)+\lambda\Sigma^{-1}(a-m)\bigr). (31)

The Gaussian factor and the lower bound on cc make the target density vanish at infinity; the polynomial growth assumptions ensure integrability. Integrating its derivative over ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} therefore gives 𝔼qm∗​[∇a​log​qm∗]=∫∇aqm∗​(a)​𝑑a=0\mathbb{E}_{q_{m}^{*}}[\nabla_{a}\log q_{m}^{*}]=\int\nabla_{a}q_{m}^{*}(a)\,\mathrm{d}a=0. Taking expectations in Eq. 31 yields

𝔼qm∗​[∇c​(a)]=λ​Σ−1​(m−m∗​(m)),\mathbb{E}_{q_{m}^{*}}[\nabla c(a)]=\lambda\Sigma^{-1}\bigl(m-m^{*}(m)\bigr), (32)

which proves the final equality for dFd_{\mathrm{F}}.

Connection to REPPO. We now consider fitting the same frozen target using reverse KL, DKL(πn∥qm∗)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{n}\|q_{m}^{*}). FERPO instead minimizes the forward KL, DKL(qm∗∥πn)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_{m}^{*}\|\pi_{n}). The following decomposition shows that reverse-KL fitting gives the same initial descent direction as REPPO, up to a positive scaling factor. Substituting the target density in Eq. 28 yields

TDKL(πn∥qm∗)=𝔼πn[c]−τH(πn)+λDKL(πn∥πm)+TlogZm.TD_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{n}\|q_{m}^{*})=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{n}}[c]-\tau H(\pi_{n})+\lambda D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{n}\|\pi_{m})+T\log Z_{m}. (33)

At n=mn=m, the KL penalty contributes no gradient, and ZmZ_{m} is independent of the candidate mean nn. Differentiating the right-hand side therefore gives REPPO’s loss gradient. Consequently, minimizing DKL(πn∥qm∗)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{n}\|q_{m}^{*}) gives the initial descent direction dR​(m)/Td_{\mathrm{R}}(m)/T: the same direction as REPPO, scaled by 1/T1/T. ∎

Shared small-variance limit. Assume additionally that cc is three-times continuously differentiable and its derivatives through order three grow at most polynomially. Fix the mean mm and positive constants τ\tau and λ\lambda. Let Σ=σ2​I\Sigma=\sigma^{2}I with σ→0\sigma\to 0. The Taylor expansion underlying the delta method (?, Appendix C) applies to both averages. Under πm\pi_{m}, 𝔼⁡[a−m]=0\mathbb{E}[a-m]=0 and 𝔼​‖a−m‖2=O⁡(σ2)\mathbb{E}\|a-m\|^{2}=O(\sigma^{2}). The target is proportional to e−c(a)/Te^{-c(a)/T} times the density of 𝒩⁡(m,(T/λ)​σ2​I)\mathcal{N}(m,(T/\lambda)\sigma^{2}I). The lower bound on cc and the growth assumptions imply 𝔼qm∗​‖a−m‖2=O⁡(σ2)\mathbb{E}_{q_{m}^{*}}\|a-m\|^{2}=O(\sigma^{2}) and 𝔼qm∗​[∇c​(a)]=O⁡(1)\mathbb{E}_{q_{m}^{*}}[\nabla c(a)]=O(1). Equation 32 then gives 𝔼qm∗​[a−m]=O⁡(σ2)\mathbb{E}_{q_{m}^{*}}[a-m]=O(\sigma^{2}). Expanding ∇c​(a)\nabla c(a) around mm therefore yields, for the initial loss gradients gR:=−dR​(m)g_{\mathrm{R}}:=-d_{\mathrm{R}}(m) and gF:=−dF​(m)g_{\mathrm{F}}:=-d_{\mathrm{F}}(m),

gR=∇c​(m)+O⁡(σ2),λ​gF=∇c​(m)+O⁡(σ2).g_{\mathrm{R}}=\nabla c(m)+O(\sigma^{2}),\qquad\lambda g_{\mathrm{F}}=\nabla c(m)+O(\sigma^{2}).

Thus both methods approach the same descent direction wherever ∇c​(m)≠0\nabla c(m)\neq 0; in one dimension, their signs agree for sufficiently small σ\sigma. This shared limit does not imply agreement at finite width, where the target can be broad or multimodal, or uniformly near stationary points. Figure 1 uses the exact expectations at finite width.

At B in Figure 1, m=−0.6m=-0.6 and σ=0.4\sigma=0.4. The expected cost derivative is 0.2840.284, while m∗​(m)≃−0.466m^{*}(m)\simeq-0.466, giving

dR=−0.284,dF≃−0.466+0.60.42=0.838.d_{\mathrm{R}}=-0.284,\qquad d_{\mathrm{F}}\simeq\frac{-0.466+0.6}{0.4^{2}}=0.838.

Thus FERPO initially moves toward the better right well while REPPO moves toward the worse left well. This is the potential benefit illustrated by the experiment: fitting the reweighted mean can give an update toward a better region even when the expected-cost gradient points elsewhere. The comparison concerns directions, not matched step sizes or eventual optimization success. It applies at the reference policy with fixed covariance.

B.5.2 Recovering the target-mean direction from samples

The update-direction comparison in Appendix B.5.1 uses the exact target mean. With SNIS, FERPO instead uses m^∗=∑iwi​ai\widehat{m}^{*}=\sum_{i}w_{i}a_{i} and the estimated negative gradient is d^F=Σ−1​(m^∗−m)\widehat{d}_{\mathrm{F}}=\Sigma^{-1}(\widehat{m}^{*}-m). The integration-by-parts identity holds for the population target; it need not hold for a finite weighted sample. In particular, SNIS is generally biased at finite KK. For a proposal rr that is positive wherever qm∗q_{m}^{*} is positive, independent samples ai∼ra_{i}\sim r receive weights

ui=e−c(ai)/Tπm(ai)λ/Tr⁡(ai),wi=ui∑juj.u_{i}=\frac{e^{-c(a_{i})/T}\pi_{m}(a_{i})^{\lambda/T}}{r(a_{i})},\qquad w_{i}=\frac{u_{i}}{\sum_{j}u_{j}}. (34)

Changing rr changes the estimate’s accuracy while preserving the same target, provided the denominator uses the actual proposal.

Proposition 4 (Accuracy of the sampled target mean).

For fixed qm∗q_{m}^{*} and rr, m^∗→m∗​(m)\widehat{m}^{*}\to m^{*}(m) almost surely as K→∞K\to\infty. If the matrix

Ωr:=∫qm∗​(a)2r⁡(a)​(a−m∗​(m))​(a−m∗​(m))⊤​𝑑a\Omega_{r}:=\int\frac{q_{m}^{*}(a)^{2}}{r(a)}(a-m^{*}(m))(a-m^{*}(m))^{\top}\,\mathrm{d}a (35)

has finite trace, then K​(m^∗−m∗​(m))⟹𝒩⁡(0,Ωr)\sqrt{K}\bigl(\widehat{m}^{*}-m^{*}(m)\bigr)\Longrightarrow\mathcal{N}(0,\Omega_{r}). Here, ⟹\Longrightarrow denotes convergence in distribution. For large KK, the estimated target mean is approximately Gaussian around the exact mean, with covariance Ωr/K\Omega_{r}/K. Thus, the typical estimation error decreases as 1/K1/\sqrt{K}, while its magnitude depends on how well the proposal covers the target distribution.

Proof.

This is the standard SNIS argument (?, Section 9.2). Let W=qm∗/rW=q_{m}^{*}/r. Then 𝔼r​W=1\mathbb{E}_{r}W=1, 𝔼r​[W​a]=m∗​(m)\mathbb{E}_{r}[Wa]=m^{*}(m), and m^∗=(∑iW⁡(ai)​ai)/(∑iW⁡(ai))\widehat{m}^{*}=(\sum_{i}W(a_{i})a_{i})/(\sum_{i}W(a_{i})). The strong law of large numbers proves consistency, since the target has a finite first moment. For the limiting distribution, write

K​(m^∗−m∗​(m))=K−1/2∑iW(ai)(ai−m∗(m))K−1​∑iW⁡(ai).\sqrt{K}(\widehat{m}^{*}-m^{*}(m))=\frac{K^{-1/2}\sum_{i}W(a_{i})(a_{i}-m^{*}(m))}{K^{-1}\sum_{i}W(a_{i})}.

The numerator summands have mean zero and covariance Ωr\Omega_{r}. The multivariate central limit theorem and convergence of the denominator to one give the result. ∎

Why a wider proposal can help. The covariance in Eq. 35 is large when the target places mass far from its mean in a region that the proposal rarely samples. Such a region contributes to the exact mean but is often absent from a finite batch. Increasing proposal density there can reduce this source of error. This explains the improvement from wider proposals in Figure 6; increasing width is useful only insofar as it improves coverage of influential target regions.

Although SNIS is consistent, finite-sample error can place the estimated target mean on the wrong side of the current policy mean, reversing the update direction.

B.6 From surrogate improvement to return improvement

Statement to be proved. We restate Eq. 3 from the main text. For a fixed temperature τ\tau, an exact rollout critic, and bounded soft advantage, define the actual return change, the surrogate loss change, and the predicted return gain as

Δ​Jτ\displaystyle\Delta J_{\tau} :=Jτ​(πθ)−Jτ​(πroll),\displaystyle:=J_{\tau}(\pi_{\theta})-J_{\tau}(\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}),
Δ​ℒME\displaystyle\Delta\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ME}} :=ℒME​(θ,θroll)−ℒME​(θroll,θroll),\displaystyle:=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ME}}(\theta;\theta_{\mathrm{roll}})-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ME}}(\theta_{\mathrm{roll}};\theta_{\mathrm{roll}}),
Δ​Jsurrogate\displaystyle\Delta J_{\mathrm{surrogate}} :=−Δ​ℒME.\displaystyle:=-\Delta\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ME}}.

Both Δ​Jτ\Delta J_{\tau} and Δ​ℒME\Delta\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ME}} are defined as candidate minus rollout. Since JτJ_{\tau} is maximized but ℒME\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ME}} is minimized, a negative loss change gives a positive predicted return gain Δ​Jsurrogate\Delta J_{\mathrm{surrogate}}. Under the assumptions detailed below, we prove the bound with a TV advantage penalty and a KL entropy correction:

Δ​Jτ\displaystyle\Delta J_{\tau} ≥Δ​Jsurrogate−4​γ​ϵA(1−γ)2​(DTVmax)2−τ1−γ​DKLmax,\displaystyle\geq\Delta J_{\mathrm{surrogate}}-\frac{4\gamma\epsilon_{A}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}(D_{\mathrm{TV}}^{\max})^{2}-\frac{\tau}{1-\gamma}D_{\mathrm{KL}}^{\max}, (3)
DTVmax\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{TV}}^{\max} :=supsDTV(πθ(⋅∣s),πroll(⋅∣s)),\displaystyle:=\sup_{s}D_{\mathrm{TV}}\!\left(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s),\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(\cdot\mid s)\right),
DKLmax\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}^{\max} :=supsDKL(πθ(⋅∣s)∥πroll(⋅∣s)).\displaystyle:=\sup_{s}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s)\middle\|\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(\cdot\mid s)\right).

Here ϵA=sups,a|Aroll​(s,a)|\epsilon_{A}=\sup_{s,a}|A_{\mathrm{roll}}(s,a)| bounds the soft advantage, defined below. If Δ​Jsurrogate\Delta J_{\mathrm{surrogate}} exceeds the sum of the two penalties, then Jτ​(πθ)>Jτ​(πroll)J_{\tau}(\pi_{\theta})>J_{\tau}(\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}).

Proof roadmap. The surrogate uses rollout states, whereas the return depends on states visited by the candidate policy. To bound the resulting prediction error, we proceed as follows.

  1. 1.

    Express the surrogate gain. Expand the KL losses in Substep 1.2, then average the resulting advantage and entropy correction over rollout states in Substep 1.4.

  2. 2.

    Express the return gain in the same form. Telescope the rollout value terms in Substep 2.2. In Substep 2.4, show that the two gains differ only in their state distributions.

  3. 3.

    Bound the advantage error. Bound the expected advantage in Substep 3.1 and the change in visited states in Substep 3.5. Combine these bounds into a TV penalty in Substep 3.6.

  4. 4.

    Complete the return-improvement bound. Bound the entropy correction in Substep 4.1, combine the two penalties in Substep 4.2, and state the sufficient condition for improvement in Substep 4.3.

We adapt the entropy-regularized performance-difference identity of ?, Lemma B.1 (Substep 2.4) and combine it with the TRPO state-distribution mismatch argument (?) (Substep 3.6).

Notation and assumptions. Keep τ\tau and πroll\pi_{\mathrm{roll}} fixed throughout the update, and let πθ\pi_{\theta} be the candidate policy. We use the main text’s Δ​Jτ\Delta J_{\tau} and Δ​Jsurrogate\Delta J_{\mathrm{surrogate}}, with a positive sign denoting improvement in both cases. The exact rollout critic defines

Aroll​(s,a)=Qroll​(s,a)−τ​log⁡πroll​(a∣s)−Vτπroll​(s),ϵA:=sups,a|Aroll​(s,a)|<∞.A_{\mathrm{roll}}(s,a)=Q_{\mathrm{roll}}(s,a)-\tau\log\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(a\mid s)-V_{\tau}^{\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}}(s),\qquad\epsilon_{A}:=\sup_{s,a}|A_{\mathrm{roll}}(s,a)|<\infty.

Its expectation under the rollout policy is zero at every state. Define

A¯θ​(s)\displaystyle\bar{A}_{\theta}(s) :=𝔼a∼πθ(⋅∣s)[Aroll(s,a)],\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s)}[A_{\mathrm{roll}}(s,a)], (36)
k⁡(s)\displaystyle k(s) :=DKL(πθ(⋅∣s)∥πroll(⋅∣s)),D:=supsk(s)=DKLmax(πθ∥πroll)<∞.\displaystyle:=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s)\middle\|\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(\cdot\mid s)\right),\qquad D:=\sup_{s}k(s)=D_{\mathrm{KL}}^{\max}(\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\mathrm{roll}})<\infty.

Here A¯θ​(s)\bar{A}_{\theta}(s) averages the rollout advantage over the candidate’s actions. The divergence k⁡(s)k(s) measures change from the rollout policy; the KL in Eq. 2 instead measures distance to the Boltzmann target. We assume the relevant discounted expectations are finite and γt​𝔼ρ0,P,πθ​[|Vτπroll​(st)|]→0\gamma^{t}\mathbb{E}_{\rho_{0},P,\pi_{\theta}}[|V_{\tau}^{\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}}(s_{t})|]\to 0. The latter condition, satisfied for bounded soft values, removes the terminal term in Substep 2.2.

Step 1: express the surrogate improvement

We show that the surrogate gain is the rollout-state average of A¯θ​(s)−τ​k​(s)\bar{A}_{\theta}(s)-\tau k(s), scaled by 1/(1−γ)1/(1-\gamma). This form will allow a direct comparison with the return gain.

Substep 1.1: Write the difference of the two losses. First, negate the candidate-minus-rollout loss change to obtain the predicted return gain, then expand it as a difference of KL divergences to the same Boltzmann target. Both surrogate losses use the same frozen critic QrollQ_{\mathrm{roll}}, Boltzmann target pQ,τp_{Q,\tau}, and state distribution drolld_{\mathrm{roll}}. Only the policy inside the KL changes. Starting from the definition of improvement in the main text and substituting Eq. 2,

Δ​Jsurrogate\displaystyle\Delta J_{\mathrm{surrogate}} =−Δ​ℒME=ℒME​(θroll,θroll)−ℒME​(θ,θroll)\displaystyle=-\Delta\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ME}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ME}}(\theta_{\mathrm{roll}};\theta_{\mathrm{roll}})-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ME}}(\theta;\theta_{\mathrm{roll}})
=τ1−γ𝔼s∼droll[DKL(πroll∥pQ,τ)−DKL(πθ∥pQ,τ)].\displaystyle=\frac{\tau}{1-\gamma}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\mathrm{roll}}}\!\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}\|p_{Q,\tau})-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}\|p_{Q,\tau})\right].

In the following per-state calculations, all action distributions and action expectations are conditional on the same state ss.

Substep 1.2: Expand the KL losses and cancel the normalizer. We turn the KL difference into a difference of entropy-augmented critic values. The target’s normalizing constant cancels because it is identical in both losses. From Eq. 17, log⁡pQ,τ​(a∣s)=Qroll​(s,a)/τ−log⁡ZQ​(s)\log p_{Q,\tau}(a\mid s)=Q_{\mathrm{roll}}(s,a)/\tau-\log Z_{Q}(s). For either π=πroll\pi=\pi_{\mathrm{roll}} or π=πθ\pi=\pi_{\theta}, this gives

=𝔼a∼π​[τ​log⁡π⁡(a∣s)−Qroll​(s,a)]+τ​log⁡ZQ​(s).\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi}\!\left[\tau\log\pi(a\mid s)-Q_{\mathrm{roll}}(s,a)\right]+\tau\log Z_{Q}(s).

The last term is outside the action expectation because it depends only on ss. Subtracting the candidate’s KL from the rollout policy’s KL now makes the cancellation explicit:

τ[DKL(πroll∥pQ,τ)−DKL(πθ∥pQ,τ)]\displaystyle\tau\bigl[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}\|p_{Q,\tau})-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}\|p_{Q,\tau})\bigr]
=𝔼a∼πroll​[τ​log⁡πroll​(a∣s)−Qroll​(s,a)]+τ​log⁡ZQ​(s)\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}}\!\left[\tau\log\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(a\mid s)-Q_{\mathrm{roll}}(s,a)\right]+\tau\log Z_{Q}(s)
−𝔼a∼πθ​[τ​log⁡πθ​(a∣s)−Qroll​(s,a)]−τ​log⁡ZQ​(s)\displaystyle-\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{\theta}}\!\left[\tau\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)-Q_{\mathrm{roll}}(s,a)\right]-\tau\log Z_{Q}(s)
=𝔼a∼πθ​[Qroll​(s,a)−τ​log⁡πθ​(a∣s)]−Vτπroll​(s).\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{\theta}}\!\left[Q_{\mathrm{roll}}(s,a)-\tau\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)\right]-V_{\tau}^{\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}}(s).

Here we used the soft-value definition from Section 2,

Vτπroll​(s)=𝔼a∼πroll​[Qroll​(s,a)−τ​log⁡πroll​(a∣s)].V_{\tau}^{\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}}(s)=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}}\!\left[Q_{\mathrm{roll}}(s,a)-\tau\log\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(a\mid s)\right].

Thus the rollout expectation in the subtraction equals −Vτπroll​(s)-V_{\tau}^{\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}}(s).

Substep 1.3: Identify the advantage and entropy correction. We now show that the remaining candidate expectation equals A¯θ​(s)−τ​k​(s)\bar{A}_{\theta}(s)-\tau k(s). Add and subtract τ​log⁡πroll​(a∣s)\tau\log\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(a\mid s) for each action:

Qroll​(s,a)−τ​log⁡πθ​(a∣s)−Vτπroll​(s)\displaystyle Q_{\mathrm{roll}}(s,a)-\tau\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)-V_{\tau}^{\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}}(s)
=Qroll​(s,a)−τ​log⁡πroll​(a∣s)−Vτπroll​(s)⏟Aroll​(s,a)−τ⁡[log⁡πθ​(a∣s)−log⁡πroll​(a∣s)]\displaystyle=\underbrace{Q_{\mathrm{roll}}(s,a)-\tau\log\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(a\mid s)-V_{\tau}^{\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}}(s)}_{A_{\mathrm{roll}}(s,a)}-\tau\bigl[\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)-\log\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(a\mid s)\bigr]
=Aroll​(s,a)−τ​log⁡πθ​(a∣s)πroll​(a∣s).\displaystyle=A_{\mathrm{roll}}(s,a)-\tau\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)}{\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(a\mid s)}.

Taking the action expectation under πθ\pi_{\theta} yields

𝔼a∼πθ​[Qroll​(s,a)−τ​log⁡πθ​(a∣s)]−Vτπroll​(s)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{\theta}}\!\left[Q_{\mathrm{roll}}(s,a)-\tau\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)\right]-V_{\tau}^{\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}}(s)
=𝔼a∼πθ​[Aroll​(s,a)]⏟A¯θ​(s)−τ𝔼a∼πθ​[log⁡πθ​(a∣s)πroll​(a∣s)]⏟DKL(πθ∥πroll)=k(s).\displaystyle=\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{\theta}}[A_{\mathrm{roll}}(s,a)]}_{\bar{A}_{\theta}(s)}-\tau\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{\theta}}\!\left[\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)}{\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(a\mid s)}\right]}_{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\mathrm{roll}})=k(s)}.

The action distribution in this expectation determines the direction of the KL: its first argument is the candidate policy.

Substep 1.4: Average over rollout states. We complete the surrogate identity by inserting the per-state result from Substep 1.3 into the loss difference from Substep 1.1:

Δ​Jsurrogate\displaystyle\Delta J_{\mathrm{surrogate}} =11−γ​𝔼s∼droll​[𝔼a∼πθ​[Qroll​(s,a)−τ​log⁡πθ​(a∣s)]−Vτπroll​(s)]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\mathrm{roll}}}\!\left[\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{\theta}}[Q_{\mathrm{roll}}(s,a)-\tau\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)]-V_{\tau}^{\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}}(s)\right] (37)
=11−γ​𝔼s∼droll​[A¯θ​(s)−τ​k​(s)].\displaystyle=\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\mathrm{roll}}}[\bar{A}_{\theta}(s)-\tau k(s)].

Thus, the surrogate gain is the candidate’s expected rollout advantage, minus the correction needed to evaluate entropy under the candidate policy.

Step 2: express the actual return improvement

We show that Δ​Jτ\Delta J_{\tau} averages the same quantity A¯θ​(s)−τ​k​(s)\bar{A}_{\theta}(s)-\tau k(s) as the surrogate, but over the candidate’s state distribution dπθd^{\pi_{\theta}}. We derive this identity directly from the return definition.

Substep 2.1: Subtract the returns using a common initial distribution. We first write the return difference as an expectation over candidate trajectories. Restating Eq. 1,

Jτ​(πθ)\displaystyle J_{\tau}(\pi_{\theta}) =11−γ​𝔼s∼dπθa∼πθ(⋅∣s)​[r⁡(s,a)−τ​log⁡πθ​(a∣s)]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}s\sim d^{\pi_{\theta}}\\ a\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s)\end{subarray}}[r(s,a)-\tau\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)]
=𝔼ρ0,P,πθ​[∑t=0∞γt​(r⁡(st,at)−τ​log⁡πθ​(at∣st))].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\rho_{0},P,\pi_{\theta}}\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}\bigl(r(s_{t},a_{t})-\tau\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid s_{t})\bigr)\right].

By definition, the rollout policy’s soft value is its expected entropy-augmented return from a given state. Hence Jτ​(πroll)=𝔼s0∼ρ0​[Vτπroll​(s0)]J_{\tau}(\pi_{\mathrm{roll}})=\mathbb{E}_{s_{0}\sim\rho_{0}}[V_{\tau}^{\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}}(s_{0})]. Both policies start from the same ρ0\rho_{0}, so this subtraction can be placed inside the expectation over candidate trajectories:

Δ​Jτ=𝔼ρ0,P,πθ​[∑t=0∞γt​(r⁡(st,at)−τ​log⁡πθ​(at∣st))−Vτπroll​(s0)].\Delta J_{\tau}=\mathbb{E}_{\rho_{0},P,\pi_{\theta}}\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}\bigl(r(s_{t},a_{t})-\tau\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid s_{t})\bigr)-V_{\tau}^{\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}}(s_{0})\right].

∑t=0Nγt​[γ​Vτπroll​(st+1)−Vτπroll​(st)]=∑t=1N+1γt​Vτπroll​(st)−∑t=0Nγt​Vτπroll​(st)\displaystyle\sum_{t=0}^{N}\gamma^{t}\bigl[\gamma V_{\tau}^{\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}}(s_{t+1})-V_{\tau}^{\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}}(s_{t})\bigr]=\sum_{t=1}^{N+1}\gamma^{t}V_{\tau}^{\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}}(s_{t})-\sum_{t=0}^{N}\gamma^{t}V_{\tau}^{\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}}(s_{t})
=−Vτπroll​(s0)+γN+1​Vτπroll​(sN+1).\displaystyle=-V_{\tau}^{\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}}(s_{0})+\gamma^{N+1}V_{\tau}^{\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}}(s_{N+1}).

This cancellation also holds along candidate trajectories: it only uses successive evaluations of the same rollout value function. Taking expectations and letting N→∞N\to\infty, the terminal term vanishes by the assumption stated above. Substituting this sum for the initial-value subtraction therefore gives

Δ​Jτ=𝔼ρ0,P,πθ​[∑t=0∞γt​(r⁡(st,at)−τ​log⁡πθ​(at∣st)+γ​Vτπroll​(st+1)−Vτπroll​(st))].\Delta J_{\tau}=\mathbb{E}_{\rho_{0},P,\pi_{\theta}}\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}\Bigl(r(s_{t},a_{t})-\tau\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid s_{t})+\gamma V_{\tau}^{\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}}(s_{t+1})-V_{\tau}^{\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}}(s_{t})\Bigr)\right].

Each summand is the reward plus entropy contribution at the current step, plus the discounted next-state value, minus the current-state value.

Substep 2.3: Evaluate the conditional one-step contribution. We show that each summand, averaged over the candidate’s action and the next state, equals A¯θ​(s)−τ​k​(s)\bar{A}_{\theta}(s)-\tau k(s). For fixed ss and aa, the rollout Bellman equation is

𝔼a∼πθ(⋅∣s)s′∼P(⋅∣s,a)​[r⁡(s,a)−τ​log⁡πθ​(a∣s)+γ​Vτπroll​(s′)−Vτπroll​(s)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}a\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s)\\ s^{\prime}\sim P(\cdot\mid s,a)\end{subarray}}\!\left[r(s,a)-\tau\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)+\gamma V_{\tau}^{\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}}(s^{\prime})-V_{\tau}^{\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}}(s)\right]
=𝔼a∼πθ(⋅∣s)[Qroll(s,a)−τlogπθ(a∣s)−Vτπroll(s)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s)}\!\left[Q_{\mathrm{roll}}(s,a)-\tau\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)-V_{\tau}^{\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}}(s)\right]
=𝔼a∼πθ(⋅∣s)[Aroll(s,a)−τlogπθ​(a∣s)πroll​(a∣s)]=A¯θ(s)−τk(s).\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s)}\!\left[A_{\mathrm{roll}}(s,a)-\tau\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)}{\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(a\mid s)}\right]=\bar{A}_{\theta}(s)-\tau k(s).

These nested averages are the law of total expectation applied to the candidate trajectories. The value functions remain those of the rollout policy throughout.

Substep 2.4: Average over candidate states and compare the gains. We now obtain the return-improvement identity and compare it with Eq. 37. At time tt, these states follow ρtπθ\rho_{t}^{\pi_{\theta}}. Using dπθ=(1−γ)​∑t≥0γt​ρtπθd^{\pi_{\theta}}=(1-\gamma)\sum_{t\geq 0}\gamma^{t}\rho_{t}^{\pi_{\theta}}, we obtain

Δ​Jτ=∑t=0∞γt​𝔼s∼ρtπθ​[A¯θ​(s)−τ​k​(s)]=11−γ​𝔼s∼dπθ​[A¯θ​(s)−τ​k​(s)].\Delta J_{\tau}=\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\rho_{t}^{\pi_{\theta}}}[\bar{A}_{\theta}(s)-\tau k(s)]=\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d^{\pi_{\theta}}}[\bar{A}_{\theta}(s)-\tau k(s)]. (38)

For a direct comparison, restate the actual return improvement and the surrogate improvement from Eq. 37:

Δ​Jτ=11−γ​𝔼s∼dπθ​[A¯θ​(s)−τ​k​(s)],Δ​Jsurrogate=11−γ​𝔼s∼droll​[A¯θ​(s)−τ​k​(s)].\Delta J_{\tau}=\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d^{\pi_{\theta}}}[\bar{A}_{\theta}(s)-\tau k(s)],\qquad\Delta J_{\mathrm{surrogate}}=\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\mathrm{roll}}}[\bar{A}_{\theta}(s)-\tau k(s)].

With an exact rollout critic and fixed temperature, the two improvements differ only in how states are weighted. Both use the candidate policy’s actions inside A¯θ​(s)\bar{A}_{\theta}(s) and k⁡(s)k(s). The surrogate evaluates the candidate policy on states visited by the rollout policy, whereas the actual return reflects states visited by the candidate itself. If these state distributions coincide, the two improvements are exactly equal. The remaining proof bounds the discrepancy caused by changing the visited states.

Step 3: bound the error in the advantage term

We bound the error from averaging A¯θ\bar{A}_{\theta} over rollout states instead of candidate states. The argument has two parts: a small policy change limits both the expected rollout advantage and the change in visited states. Their product gives the advantage penalty in Eq. 3.

Substep 3.1: Bound the expected rollout advantage. We show that |A¯θ​(s)|≤2​ϵA​α|\bar{A}_{\theta}(s)|\leq 2\epsilon_{A}\alpha, where α\alpha is the largest policy change in total variation. Recall ϵA\epsilon_{A} and define α\alpha by

α\displaystyle\alpha :=supsDTV(πθ(⋅∣s),πroll(⋅∣s))=12sups∫𝒜|πθ(a∣s)−πroll(a∣s)|da.\displaystyle:=\sup_{s}D_{\mathrm{TV}}\!\left(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s),\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(\cdot\mid s)\right)=\frac{1}{2}\sup_{s}\int_{\mathcal{A}}|\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)-\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(a\mid s)|\,\mathrm{d}a.

≤∫𝒜|πθ​(a∣s)−πroll​(a∣s)|​|Aroll​(s,a)|​𝑑a\displaystyle\leq\int_{\mathcal{A}}|\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)-\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(a\mid s)||A_{\mathrm{roll}}(s,a)|\,\mathrm{d}a
≤ϵA​∫𝒜|πθ​(a∣s)−πroll​(a∣s)|​da≤2​ϵA​α.\displaystyle\leq\epsilon_{A}\int_{\mathcal{A}}|\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)-\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(a\mid s)|\,\mathrm{d}a\leq 2\epsilon_{A}\alpha.

Substep 3.2: Derive the balance equation for discounted visits. This identity separates the initial visit from all later visits. We begin by defining the one-step transition operator PπP_{\pi}. Starting at state ss, first draw an action from π(⋅∣s)\pi(\cdot\mid s), then draw the next state from P(⋅∣s,a)P(\cdot\mid s,a). Averaging over the action gives the next-state distribution under the policy:

Pπ​(s′∣s):=∫𝒜π⁡(a∣s)​P​(s′∣s,a)​𝑑a.P_{\pi}(s^{\prime}\mid s):=\int_{\mathcal{A}}\pi(a\mid s)P(s^{\prime}\mid s,a)\,\mathrm{d}a.

(ρ​Pπ)​(s′):=∫ρ⁡(s)​Pπ​(s′∣s)​𝑑s.(\rho P_{\pi})(s^{\prime}):=\int\rho(s)P_{\pi}(s^{\prime}\mid s)\,\mathrm{d}s.

dπ:=(1−γ)​∑t=0∞γt​ρtπ=(1−γ)​ρ0+(1−γ)​∑t=1∞γt​ρtπ.d^{\pi}:=(1-\gamma)\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}\rho_{t}^{\pi}=(1-\gamma)\rho_{0}+(1-\gamma)\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}\rho_{t}^{\pi}.

Thus it collects visits from time 11 onward. Adding the initial visit gives

dπ=(1−γ)​ρ0+γ​dπ​Pπ.d^{\pi}=(1-\gamma)\rho_{0}+\gamma d^{\pi}P_{\pi}.

We express the difference in visited states as two contributions: propagation of an existing state difference, and the effect of choosing different actions. Apply the balance equation from Substep 3.2 to each policy. Both policies use the same ρ0\rho_{0}, so their initial-state terms cancel. The first term propagates the difference in current-state distributions through the same candidate transition kernel. The second starts from the same rollout state distribution and measures the effect of changing the policy’s action probabilities. We bound these two contributions separately below.

‖δ​d​Pπθ‖1=∫|∫δ​d​(s)​Pπθ​(s′∣s)​𝑑s|​d​s′≤∫|δ​d​(s)|​[∫Pπθ​(s′∣s)​d​s′]⏟1​𝑑s=‖δ​d‖1.\|\delta dP_{\pi_{\theta}}\|_{1}=\int\left|\int\delta d(s)P_{\pi_{\theta}}(s^{\prime}\mid s)\,\mathrm{d}s\right|\,\mathrm{d}s^{\prime}\leq\int|\delta d(s)|\underbrace{\left[\int P_{\pi_{\theta}}(s^{\prime}\mid s)\,\mathrm{d}s^{\prime}\right]}_{1}\,\mathrm{d}s=\|\delta d\|_{1}.

≤∫𝒜|πθ​(a∣s)−πroll​(a∣s)|​[∫P⁡(s′∣s,a)​d​s′]⏟1​da≤2​α.\displaystyle\leq\int_{\mathcal{A}}|\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)-\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(a\mid s)|\underbrace{\left[\int P(s^{\prime}\mid s,a)\,\mathrm{d}s^{\prime}\right]}_{1}\,\mathrm{d}a\leq 2\alpha.

11−γ​|𝔼dπθ​[A¯θ]−𝔼droll​[A¯θ]|\displaystyle\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\left|\mathbb{E}_{d^{\pi_{\theta}}}[\bar{A}_{\theta}]-\mathbb{E}_{d_{\mathrm{roll}}}[\bar{A}_{\theta}]\right| ≤‖dπθ−droll‖1​sups|A¯θ​(s)|1−γ\displaystyle\leq\frac{\|d^{\pi_{\theta}}-d_{\mathrm{roll}}\|_{1}\sup_{s}|\bar{A}_{\theta}(s)|}{1-\gamma} (41)
≤4​γ​ϵA(1−γ)2​α2.\displaystyle\leq\frac{4\gamma\epsilon_{A}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}\alpha^{2}.

This step bounds the contribution of the advantage term to the discrepancy between Δ​Jτ\Delta J_{\tau} and Δ​Jsurrogate\Delta J_{\mathrm{surrogate}}. Small policy changes limit both the change in visited states and the expected rollout advantage, producing the quadratic total-variation bound above. Step 4 accounts for the remaining entropy correction.

Step 4: complete the return-improvement bound

We bound the remaining entropy correction and add it to the advantage error. This proves Eq. 3 and gives a sufficient condition for JτJ_{\tau} to improve.

Substep 4.1: Bound the entropy correction. Subtracting the two gain identities from Substep 2.4, the contribution from −τ​k​(s)-\tau k(s) is τ1−γ​(𝔼droll​[k]−𝔼dπθ​[k])\frac{\tau}{1-\gamma}(\mathbb{E}_{d_{\mathrm{roll}}}[k]-\mathbb{E}_{d^{\pi_{\theta}}}[k]). We show that this contribution is at least −τD/(1−γ)-\tau D/(1-\gamma). Since 0≤k⁡(s)≤D0\leq k(s)\leq D, both state averages lie in [0,D][0,D]. Hence

τ1−γ​(𝔼s∼droll​[k⁡(s)]−𝔼s∼dπθ​[k⁡(s)])≥−τ1−γ​D.\frac{\tau}{1-\gamma}\left(\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\mathrm{roll}}}[k(s)]-\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d^{\pi_{\theta}}}[k(s)]\right)\geq-\frac{\tau}{1-\gamma}D.

Substep 4.2: Combine the advantage and entropy bounds. We obtain the claimed lower bound on Δ​Jτ\Delta J_{\tau} by subtracting the two gain identities and applying Substep 3.6 to the advantage term, then Substep 4.1 to the entropy term:

Δ​Jτ≥\displaystyle\Delta J_{\tau}\geq{} Δ​Jsurrogate−4​γ​ϵA(1−γ)2​α2+τ1−γ​(𝔼s∼droll​[k⁡(s)]−𝔼s∼dπθ​[k⁡(s)])\displaystyle\Delta J_{\mathrm{surrogate}}-\frac{4\gamma\epsilon_{A}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}\alpha^{2}+\frac{\tau}{1-\gamma}\left(\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\mathrm{roll}}}[k(s)]-\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d^{\pi_{\theta}}}[k(s)]\right) (42)
≥\displaystyle\geq{} Δ​Jsurrogate−4​γ​ϵA(1−γ)2​α2−τ1−γ​D.\displaystyle\Delta J_{\mathrm{surrogate}}-\frac{4\gamma\epsilon_{A}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}\alpha^{2}-\frac{\tau}{1-\gamma}D.

This proves Eq. 3. The first penalty bounds the error in the advantage prediction; the second bounds the error in its entropy correction. Both arise from evaluating the update on rollout states instead of the states visited by the candidate.

Substep 4.3: State the improvement condition and its practical meaning. The bound guarantees an increase in JτJ_{\tau} when the surrogate gain exceeds the two error penalties. Explicitly,

Δ​Jsurrogate>4​γ​ϵA(1−γ)2​α2+τ1−γ​D⟹Jτ​(πθ)>Jτ​(πroll).\Delta J_{\mathrm{surrogate}}>\frac{4\gamma\epsilon_{A}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}\alpha^{2}+\frac{\tau}{1-\gamma}D\quad\Longrightarrow\quad J_{\tau}(\pi_{\theta})>J_{\tau}(\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}).

To express a sufficient condition using only KL, apply Pinsker’s inequality, 2​α2≤D2\alpha^{2}\leq D:

4​γ​ϵA(1−γ)2​α2+τ1−γ​D≤(2​γ​ϵA(1−γ)2+τ1−γ)​D.\frac{4\gamma\epsilon_{A}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}\alpha^{2}+\frac{\tau}{1-\gamma}D\leq\left(\frac{2\gamma\epsilon_{A}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}+\frac{\tau}{1-\gamma}\right)D.

The surrogate gain exceeding this KL upper bound is therefore also sufficient for return improvement. In words, the predicted improvement must exceed the bound on the prediction error. A small KL alone does not imply improvement, and failing this sufficient condition does not imply that the update is harmful.

This motivates the KL term in Eq. 4: minimize the surrogate while limiting policy change. Replacing the worst-state KL constraint by a rollout-average constraint gives the average penalty. With the critic and rollout distribution fixed, the full Lagrangian satisfies

ℒ⁡(πθ,τ,λ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\pi_{\theta},\tau,\lambda) =(1−γ)​ℒME​(θ,θroll)+λ​𝔼s∼droll​[k⁡(s)]\displaystyle=(1-\gamma)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ME}}(\theta;\theta_{\mathrm{roll}})+\lambda\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\mathrm{roll}}}[k(s)]
+τ​ℋtarget−λ​δKL−τ​𝔼s∼droll​[log⁡ZQ​(s)].\displaystyle+\tau\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{target}}-\lambda\delta_{\mathrm{KL}}-\tau\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\mathrm{roll}}}[\log Z_{Q}(s)].

The second line is independent of the policy when the multipliers are fixed. The average constraint is a practical relaxation. With this relaxation and an estimated critic, minimizing ℒ\mathcal{L} over the policy does not by itself guarantee the sufficient condition above.

B.7 Trust regions for Gaussian policies

For Gaussian policies, a bound on either KL direction also bounds the other. A TV bound strictly below one bounds both KL directions. The short proofs below give conservative constants sufficient to control the entropy correction in Eq. 3.

Setup and notation. Fix a state and suppress the conditioning on ss. Assume positive-definite covariances, meaning every variance is strictly positive for our diagonal Gaussian policies, and use natural logarithms. KL and TV are unchanged by a common invertible transformation: its Jacobian cancels in the density ratio and the integral. We can therefore undo the common tanh squashing and action rescaling, then subtract the rollout mean and divide by the rollout standard deviation in each coordinate. In these standardized coordinates,

πroll=𝒩⁡(0,I),πcurr=𝒩⁡(m,diag⁡(σ12,…,σd2)).\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}=\mathcal{N}(0,I),\qquad\pi_{\mathrm{curr}}=\mathcal{N}\!\left(m,\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_{1}^{2},\ldots,\sigma_{d}^{2})\right).

Here mim_{i} is the standardized mean change, and σi2\sigma_{i}^{2} is the current variance relative to the rollout variance. Full covariance matrices reduce to the same form by whitening and rotation. The Gaussian KL formulas separate variance changes from mean changes:

DKL(πroll∥πcurr)\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}\|\pi_{\mathrm{curr}}) =12​∑i[log⁡σi2+1σi2−1+mi2σi2],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i}\left[\log\sigma_{i}^{2}+\frac{1}{\sigma_{i}^{2}}-1+\frac{m_{i}^{2}}{\sigma_{i}^{2}}\right], (43)
DKL(πcurr∥πroll)\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\mathrm{curr}}\|\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}) =12​∑i[σi2−1−log⁡σi2+mi2].\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i}\left[\sigma_{i}^{2}-1-\log\sigma_{i}^{2}+m_{i}^{2}\right].

Each variance term and each mean term is nonnegative.

B.7.1 Forward KL bounds reverse KL

Suppose DKL(πroll∥πcurr)≤δD_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}\|\pi_{\mathrm{curr}})\leq\delta. We prove the explicit bound

DKL(πcurr∥πroll)≤δe1+2​δ.\boxed{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\mathrm{curr}}\|\pi_{\mathrm{roll}})\leq\delta e^{1+2\delta}.} (44)

This bound tends to zero with δ\delta and does not depend on the action dimension. A sharper bound is given by ?, Theorem 1.

Step 1: bound the variance ratios. Since every contribution to forward KL is nonnegative,

log⁡σi2+1σi2−1≤2​δ.\log\sigma_{i}^{2}+\frac{1}{\sigma_{i}^{2}}-1\leq 2\delta.

Rearranging and using 1/σi2>01/\sigma_{i}^{2}>0 gives

log⁡σi2≤1+2​δ−1σi2≤1+2​δ.\log\sigma_{i}^{2}\leq 1+2\delta-\frac{1}{\sigma_{i}^{2}}\leq 1+2\delta.

Exponentiating preserves the inequality, so

σi2≤e1+2​δ=:Mδ.\sigma_{i}^{2}\leq e^{1+2\delta}=:M_{\delta}.

This is a conservative upper bound on the variance; the corresponding standard deviation satisfies σi≤e1/2+δ\sigma_{i}\leq e^{1/2+\delta}.

Step 2: compare the KL terms. For any x>0x>0,

x−1−log⁡x≤max⁡{1,x}​(x−1−1+log⁡x).x-1-\log x\leq\max\{1,x\}\bigl(x^{-1}-1+\log x\bigr). (45)

To see this, both scalar expressions vanish at x=1x=1, and the derivative of the left expression is xx times the derivative of x−1−1+log⁡xx^{-1}-1+\log x. Integrating between 11 and xx bounds this factor by max⁡{1,x}\max\{1,x\}. Apply Eq. 45 with x=σi2x=\sigma_{i}^{2}. Step 1 gives both Mδ≥1M_{\delta}\geq 1 and σi2≤Mδ\sigma_{i}^{2}\leq M_{\delta}, so max⁡{1,σi2}≤Mδ\max\{1,\sigma_{i}^{2}\}\leq M_{\delta}. Thus the variance contribution in each coordinate satisfies

σi2−1−log⁡σi2\displaystyle\sigma_{i}^{2}-1-\log\sigma_{i}^{2} ≤max⁡{1,σi2}​(1σi2−1+log⁡σi2)\displaystyle\leq\max\{1,\sigma_{i}^{2}\}\left(\frac{1}{\sigma_{i}^{2}}-1+\log\sigma_{i}^{2}\right)
≤Mδ​(1σi2−1+log⁡σi2).\displaystyle\leq M_{\delta}\left(\frac{1}{\sigma_{i}^{2}}-1+\log\sigma_{i}^{2}\right).

mi2=σi2​mi2σi2≤Mδ​mi2σi2.m_{i}^{2}=\sigma_{i}^{2}\frac{m_{i}^{2}}{\sigma_{i}^{2}}\leq M_{\delta}\frac{m_{i}^{2}}{\sigma_{i}^{2}}.

Add these two inequalities in each coordinate, then sum over ii. The same MδM_{\delta} applies to every coordinate, so it factors out:

DKL(πcurr∥πroll)\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\mathrm{curr}}\|\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}) =12​∑i[σi2−1−log⁡σi2+mi2]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i}\left[\sigma_{i}^{2}-1-\log\sigma_{i}^{2}+m_{i}^{2}\right]
≤12​∑i[Mδ​(1σi2−1+log⁡σi2)+Mδ​mi2σi2]\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i}\left[M_{\delta}\left(\frac{1}{\sigma_{i}^{2}}-1+\log\sigma_{i}^{2}\right)+M_{\delta}\frac{m_{i}^{2}}{\sigma_{i}^{2}}\right]
=Mδ​12​∑i[log⁡σi2+1σi2−1+mi2σi2]\displaystyle=M_{\delta}\,\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i}\left[\log\sigma_{i}^{2}+\frac{1}{\sigma_{i}^{2}}-1+\frac{m_{i}^{2}}{\sigma_{i}^{2}}\right]
=MδDKL(πroll∥πcurr)≤Mδδ.\displaystyle=M_{\delta}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}\|\pi_{\mathrm{curr}})\leq M_{\delta}\delta.

B.7.2 TV bounds both KL directions

At a fixed state, Gaussians with positive-definite covariances satisfy ρ:=DTV​(πroll,πcurr)<1\rho:=D_{\mathrm{TV}}(\pi_{\mathrm{roll}},\pi_{\mathrm{curr}})<1. Let BG​(δ)B_{\mathrm{G}}(\delta) denote the dimension-independent reverse-KL bound given a forward-KL budget δ\delta, established by ?, Theorem 1. This bound is finite and tends to zero with δ\delta. Writing tρ=−2​log⁡(1−ρ)t_{\rho}=-2\log(1-\rho), we obtain the following corollary:

max{DKL(πcurr∥πroll),DKL(πroll∥πcurr)}≤2​BG​(tρ)+tρ⏟CTV​(ρ).\boxed{\max\!\left\{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\mathrm{curr}}\|\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}),D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}\|\pi_{\mathrm{curr}})\right\}\leq\underbrace{2B_{\mathrm{G}}(t_{\rho})+t_{\rho}}_{C_{\mathrm{TV}}(\rho)}.} (46)

Proof. Define the affinity and normalized geometric mean

A=∫πroll​(a)​πcurr​(a)​𝑑a,πmid​(a)=πroll​(a)​πcurr​(a)A.A=\int\sqrt{\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(a)\pi_{\mathrm{curr}}(a)}\,\mathrm{d}a,\qquad\pi_{\mathrm{mid}}(a)=\frac{\sqrt{\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}(a)\pi_{\mathrm{curr}}(a)}}{A}.

The distribution πmid\pi_{\mathrm{mid}} is Gaussian because its log density is quadratic. The TV–Hellinger inequality gives A≥1−ρA\geq 1-\rho (?, Section 2). Substituting the definition of πmid\pi_{\mathrm{mid}} yields

DKL(πmid∥πroll)+DKL(πmid∥πcurr)=−2logA≤tρ.D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\mathrm{mid}}\|\pi_{\mathrm{roll}})+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\mathrm{mid}}\|\pi_{\mathrm{curr}})=-2\log A\leq t_{\rho}.

Both terms are nonnegative, so each is at most tρt_{\rho}. Zhang et al.’s theorem therefore gives DKL(πcurr∥πmid)≤BG(tρ)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\mathrm{curr}}\|\pi_{\mathrm{mid}})\leq B_{\mathrm{G}}(t_{\rho}). Finally, the same density identity implies

DKL(πcurr∥πroll)\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\mathrm{curr}}\|\pi_{\mathrm{roll}}) =2DKL(πcurr∥πmid)−2logA\displaystyle=2D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\mathrm{curr}}\|\pi_{\mathrm{mid}})-2\log A
≤2​BG​(tρ)+tρ.\displaystyle\leq 2B_{\mathrm{G}}(t_{\rho})+t_{\rho}.

Exchanging the policies proves the other direction. □\square

Thus CTV​(ρ)C_{\mathrm{TV}}(\rho) is finite for every ρ<1\rho<1 and tends to zero as ρ→0\rho\to 0. A common invertible tanh transformation preserves both divergences. Applying this result uniformly across states requires a common TV bound strictly below one.

B.7.3 Implications for the return bound

If the forward-KL budget δ\delta holds at every state, Pinsker and Eq. 44 give (DTVmax)2≤δ/2(D_{\mathrm{TV}}^{\max})^{2}\leq\delta/2 and DKLmax≤δ​e1+2​δD_{\mathrm{KL}}^{\max}\leq\delta e^{1+2\delta}. A uniform TV budget ρ<1\rho<1 instead gives DKLmax≤CTV​(ρ)D_{\mathrm{KL}}^{\max}\leq C_{\mathrm{TV}}(\rho). Thus either constraint controls both penalties in Eq. 3. Small temperature further reduces the entropy penalty. The exact-critic and bounded-soft-advantage assumptions still apply, and the surrogate gain must exceed the penalties to guarantee improvement.

These are uniform, population-level statements. REPPO’s sampled forward-KL constraint (?) and FERPO’s state-average ESS objective do not establish worst-state control. For FERPO, the fitting condition of Proposition 1 and a population ESS floor e∞(s)≥e0>e−1/2e_{\infty}(s)\geq e_{0}>e^{-1/2} at every state would give DTVmax≤−2​log⁡e0<1D_{\mathrm{TV}}^{\max}\leq\sqrt{-2\log e_{0}}<1; the TV result then also bounds the entropy-related KL. These comparisons concern the two Gaussian actors; the unrestricted target q∗q^{*} need not be Gaussian.
